Fur the St. Croix Avis,. the voluntary principle. A Petition in circulation in this Town is in its way a curiosity, as the mooter of it is in himself unique. The subject of the Petition is the organization of a voluntary thor is palpably a " disappointed" Officer, who Braadcorps, and the auputs us much in mind of Reynard who lost his tail. We may consider it no bad sign for the general state of public feeling in this Island, that the newspaper has stood still on this occasion. Were such not the case, we should be lost in surmise as to the source whence the Petition referred to proceeded. Knowing, on the contrary, what is notorious, people would have been perplexed and impatient at the non-production of such extravagances. The Petition we more immediately allude to contains a double aggression þÿ first, on an absent person, and secondly, on certain individuals among those who have always acted up to (heir duty. In the first place, the attack, to say the least of it, is dastardly ; in the second, it is formed, is based on the disorganized state of iniquitous. The Petition, if we are correctly in- " the St. Thomas Brandeorps, which has been proved by the two last Fires." Now, as well-authenticated facts are more forcible and conclusive than gratuitous assertions, we shall in the following prove by such facts, to the confusion of the infatuated writer, how utterly groundless his assertions are. We will not, for obvious reasons, enter at present on the discussion of the materiel or personnel of the Brandcorps. We stall stick to the " two last Fires."

" Between two and three o'clock yesterday morning," says the Times of the 2d instant, "an alarm of Fire aroused the Inhabitants of our Town, and on proceeding to the spot it was found that the devouring element had full possession of a range of small stores on the Lot No. 16 ,( 17, the property of Ms. A. R. Liggett." The building forms (the side and end walls remain standing) a Parallelogram , 50 feet by 33 feet, the Eastcnd is separated by an alley of 6 feet from a two-story wall house with pine window shutters, and the Westend joined to a two story wall building with pine window shutters likewise. The roof was a pitch one, or triangular formed. In less than 10 minutes after the Alarm gun was fired from the Fort, tire Brandcorps Patent Metal Fire Engine No. 1 arrived at the conflagration, drawn by several members of the Brandcorps and few volunteers þÿ (there bye the bye soon took french leave) þÿ under the command of two Officers of the Brandcorps, one of whom at once assumed the command of the Brandcorps Patent Metal Fire Engine No. 4, being drawn to the spot by some gentlemen residing mostly in the immediate vicinity of the Fire. The first mentioned Engine was placed at the North West Corner of the burning building, and remained there until the Fire was extinguished. This Engine was worked by the members attached to it and volunteers. The pipe was under the direction of Mr. S. T. of the Brandcorps, who stood to it manfully and effectively, and thus saved the adjoining build-
ing to the West, from falling a prev to the flames

a jr m Mis: A T 1 The other Engine was stationed ut the N. W. corner of the house on fire, where it remained from first to last, and poured its copious streams on the wall building to the East, which likewise was rescued from tire jaws of the devouring monster. This Engine was after the first spell worked by Firemen ; tire pipe was held by Private L. I. G. of the Brandcorps, and another individual, whose efforts and indefatigable perseverance were certainly laudable. At the S. E. and S. W. corners of the burning building were stationed the Military Engine and another Engine, the property of a private Gentleman of this place. The eminent service rendered on the occasion by the officers and men attached to these Engines has received its meed of praise. Late in the morning after the roof of the building had fallen in the Engine of the French War Steamer was brought and placed likewise at the N. E. corner, and contributed effectively in extinguishing the burning mass inside of the walls. The Brand Corps Fire Engines No. 2 43, fully manned and ready for action, were kept in reserve opposite to the building to the East At the Fire there were the Chief and nine or ten other commissioned officers, (we allude not to those en masque,) besides the non-commissioned officers, firemen, and musketeers of the St. Thomas Brandcorps, who with few solitary exceptions did their duty ; for their conduct has been appreciated by the Chief of the Brand Corps, represented by the Chief Officer in this Island, and applauded by His Excellency the

Governor in Chief at St. Croix. Such are the " stubborn facts" in connexion with the one of " the last Fires." It is thus evident, that the Brandcorps was not then in a state of disorganization. But perhaps this was the case at the very last Fire. " The community," we quote from the Times of the 6th instant, " was unfortunately again thrown into a temporary state of excitemeut on Saturday night last, between twelve and one o'clock, by the ringing (striking) of the fire bell at Fort Christian, but as there could not be seen any smoke, still less any blaze, many persons were long in leaving their dwellings Immediately on the Manager of the Apothecary Hall repairing to the spot, he discovered that the building being so very isolated, and the Phosphorus having no materials within its reach to feed on, it might have been left to consume itself in perfect satety. He, nevertheless, immediately caused a cart load or two of sand to be thrown upon it, and shoveled into some large Earthen jars."þÿ Consequently there was no use for any Fire Euginc here ; yet the Brand Corps Engine No. 1 was conveyed as soon as possible by members of the Corps to the spot. The others were countermanded in the way. The Chief and some other Officers and men repaired to the "Fire." Certainly it was neither at this fire, that the Brand Corps proved itself in a state of disorganization. Now, we beg to ask the impartial reader, every rational being, and every man, who has not taken a strong doze of self-conceit, vanity, and iniquity

þÿ what more exertions and activity could be expected from the Brand Corps at the Fire of the 1st instant, us notwithstanding when the "alarm of Fire aroused the Inhabitants of our Town, the devouring clement had full possession of the building," only this house was burnt ; the adjoining house as well as the one in the East was saved ? Admitting, however, for the " sake of argument, that the Fire was conquered more by volunteers than by the established Corps" whose commands did they obey, whose directions did they follow ? Those of the Brand Major and of his officers ! What is the plea of this iniquity of the writer of the petition ? Rottwilt, the ministerial candidate, has been elected president of the Folkelhing by 58 against 25 votes. The New York Heraldx June 25, 1853. The Paris Debate gives the following resume of the last accounts from the F.ast : þÿ " We h ive received letters from Constantinople brought to Marseilles by the Leonidas. They come down to the 25th ult., and are consequently two days later than the last accounts. If we were to judge of the future by the state of the public mind there would be much reason to fear for the maintenance of peace ; hut it must not he forgotten that it is no longer on the banks of the Bosphorous but at St. Petersburg that the question will lie solved. After having nobly done its duty, the government of the Sultan has now only to wait ; but it is not from it that will come the resolution which Europe waits for with a very legitimate impatience. All that the Porte can do is to think of organizing its means of defence and although the Divan believes, with reason, in an amicable solution of the present difficulties, the news and the reports of war which every day reach it from Southern Russia, impose on it the obligation to arm itself. This, therefore, is what the Sultan is occupying himself in doing with the greatest activity; he is placing bis fleet on a war footing, be is having ammunition prepared in the arsenals, lie lias called for the contingent ofllie Viceroy of Egypt ; he has ordered the mobilization of the militia in the province of Roumelia, which, it is said, will furnish 90,000 men, and he reckons on being able, before the end of June, to assemble 120,000 men under the walls of Schumia, in or-

der to defend the line of the Balkan, for the idea of being able to dispute that of the Danube lias been abandoned. The fortresses, which were dismantled in the campaigns of 1828 and 1829, have not been repaired, and can now be considered only as open places. The news which had reached Constantinople from Odessa, Bessarabia, and the mouths of the Danube, justifies this activity and these measures of prudence. On the 24th, the eve of the departure of the Leonidas, a Russian packet, which left Odessa on the 21st arrived with the most alarming news. The Russian troops were everywhere in motion, marching towards the south, and they were said to he animated with the most lively enthusiasm. They believed that they were marching to the conquest Constantinople and of St. Sophia þÿ that j dream of all the members of the Greek Church. It was positively stated that

on the 21st, the very day of the depar. lure of the packet, the Grand Duke Constantine, second son of the Emperor Nicholas, and Grand Admiral of Russia, arrived at Odessa, in order to press forward the armaments of Sehastopol, and the departure of a numerous flotilla of gun boats for the Danube. Private letters from Ismail, of Russian Bessarabia, on the Danube, announce that accommodation has been prepared there for the Emperor Nicholas himself, who would only await the return of Prince Menschikofl to proceed in person to the Southern part of his empire. On the other hand, a courier despatched by the English Consul at Galatz to Constantinople, announced on the 24th that 20,000 bullock wagons had been put in requisition in Moldavia for the passage of the army across that province, and that these means of transport were prepared all along the banks of the Pruth. All the materiel necessary for the construction of a bridge of boats across the Danube was ready at Ismail and it was supposed that if the Russian army made an offensive movement, it would be by crossing the Danube from Ismail to Touldscha, where it would enter on the Turkish frontier, as it did in 1828, and in that case, it could in a few days be on the road to Adrianople. Touldscha is a town of Bulgaria, situate at about 150 leagues from Constantinople. We publish all these accounts without in any way guaranteeing their authenticity; for we do not believe thein to he all exact, although they come to us from a good

source. We have some doubts as to the arrival of the Grand Duke Constantine at Odessa on the 21st ult. A telegraphic despatch was received a few days since from that town, dated the 24lh, which announced the arrival of Prince Mensohikoff, but which said not a word of the journey of the Grand Duke. This is not a positive proof that lie was not at Odessa, on the 21st, but it is nevertheless a strong presumptive one. It is known that the Prince left Constantinople on the 21st. On the previous day M. de Lacour went to Bujukdere, in the Heron steamer, to take leave of the Russian Ambassador. The Prince landed from his steamer to receive him at the Russian palace. The reception given to the French Ambassador was most gracious, and when he left, the Prince accompanied him as far as the landing place. Lord ltedclifle, who, it was said, had had a rather warm altercation with the Prince, did not pay him any visit. These incidents were much talked of at Constantinople. A strong movement in public opinion was apparent at Constantinople in favor of the Sultan, not only among the Turks, but also among the Greeks, who appear to fear the protectorate of Russia much more than the suzerainty of the Ottomans."

The Chinese collection at the Dublin Exhibition presents few objects beyond the well known vases, fans, gause lanterns, ivory carvings, and grotesque paintings; the only things worthy of special notice being a porcelain landmark, a watchman's alarum, and a linger warming furnace. The land mark is about one foot and a half long, afoot wide, and three inches thick. These landmarks are used by the Chinese to point out the boundaries of estates and but for the high penalty attached to the removal of them, they offered little protection against encroachment. The watchman's alarum consists of a hollowed piece of wood, with a handle, and by striking on it with a stick, a sound is produced sufficiently loud to arouse the nearest guardian of the night. The finger-warming furnace serves the purpose of gloves, which are now worn in China, but it is of course only put in requisition in cold weather, and in the northern parts of the country. The whole collection is contributed by .Mr. llcvvett of Fen-church street, London, and though it presents a few objects that most English visitors arc not familiar with, yet even to them it will hecome a source of interest, as affording an immediate means of comparison with the productions from Japan. Of porcelain manufactures the Japanese collection contains nothing to compare with those of China. A 1 1 the porcelain articles arc limited to a few tea

cups, which, however, without exhibiting any elaborate finish or ornament, show, by the quality of the ware and the delicacy of its substance, that the Japanese have attained great perfection in the art. The beautiful Chinese carvings in ivory and sandal- wood have nothing to rival them in the Japanese collection which does not boast of a single article of the kind. The japanned cabinets, chests, and tables ol the Chinese arc much more richly inlaid and decorated ; and their gauze lanterns arc also more highly finished than the oiled paper lanters of Japan, distended with hoops of spliced bamboo. On comparing all the ornamental works of the two countries a much higher degree of finish, accompanied with greater taste for gilded decorations, appears in those of China; whilst the simpler taste of the Japanese presents in at all works greater perfection the same time of utility. Their maps are quite remarkable for exhibiting, in many instances, bird's-eye views of the country and towns, on the same principle as the pictorial surveying which was introduced into England by Mr. Horner, the artist of the Panorama of London, shown at the Colosseum. The Japanese appear to have a good notion of perspective, of which the Chinese artists have no idea ; accordingly, in the bird's-eye views, the perspective effects are well managed, though certain gaps between the middle distance and the hack-ground leave much to the imagination to supply. A map of Japan hears evidence of European light having

been thrown on this branch of their acquirements, for the points of the compass are roughly depicted in the manner of our maps with a fleur-de-lis , or something like it, at the cardinal point. In drawing and modelling the human figure also, the specimens from Japan show less deformity and much more spirited execution than the grotesque caricatures of the Chinese. The works of embroidery are nearly equal, and it is a curious coincidence that during the prevalent passion for Chinese fowls, the subjects of the principal pieces of embroidery from both countries should he cocks, and like that of English breed, without the Dutch shaped feather breeches of the highly estimated birds. Among other marks of superior advancement in civilization whieh the Japanese collection exhibits, may be noticed a capital mariner's compass of tlic usual size, a pair of well adjusted scales, with an index fixed to the beam, and, though last not least, a bank note. The circulation of paper money may he taken as evidence of the existence of public confidence and credit, and combined with the issue of gold coins of the high value of .£50, shows that the commercial transactions of Japan arc conducted on a scale approaching that of civilized nations. The Japanese appear to he a more practical and business like people than the Chinese ; and though thev seem to indulge a strange taste for monstrosities, as shown by the stuffed Hying monkey and the baboon headed snake, they do not crush the hones of the living human

foot into a valnut shell. The Japanese walking shoe is made of japanned wood, raised from the ground by two supports of the same material, and it is held to the foot by an elastic hand through which the toes pass. There is one remarkable specimen in the Japanese collection that indicates intercourse with Europe, and a taste for imitation in a mariner quite unexpected. It is a medallion head in papier niaclie, over which appears in hold Roman capitals the words "Jean Milton."

We have adopted the ' Bloomer' be, as possessing a corrupt mind and an impure because we do not like to carry from morning till night suspended from our waist, from two to four pounds of cotton and a bolt of calico, which we too grievous to be borne. If, as you say, ' the have to lift at every step we take þÿ it is a burden long dress and four pound petticoat is productive of much sickness and death,' why don't you come out and be our champion and advocate the uni- versal adoption of the ' Bloomer costume ?' Turkey. þÿ The French fleet left its anchorage at Tenedos to join that of England in Besika Bay ; the former consisted of nine vessels of various sizes and three steamers. The Turkish army was being concentrated around Adrianople; the Seraskier was about to leave Constantinople, accompanied by several generals. The feast of the Ramazan had commenced, but the works were not interrupted on that account The arrival of the French and English fleets in the Bay of Besika, and the good accord which prevails among them, inspire Turkey with the greatest confidence.

The Russian þÿArmy. -A Warsaw journal contains the following statement of the force of the Russian army : þÿ It consists of 72 regiments of infantry, divided into 32 battalions, and 24 regiments of cavalry of 1 92 squadrons ; the artillery consists of six corps and 690 guns. The total number of the active army is 290,000, without counting the reserve. The reserve is composed of six divisions of infantry and six brigades of cavalry, and forms a force of 80,000 men, without counting the pulks of Cossacks.

The "AVIS." Christiansted , Tuesday the 26 th July 1853. The " Depa rtementstidend e '' contains the following protest and Royal resolution : Under the session of the Wcstindia Colonial Council for last year, it was moved by the 3d member for the St. Thomas district, Mr. Degout, that the Council should approach His Majesty the King, with a most submissive petition containing a protest, against the question, mooted by certain members of the Diet, regarding the sale of the Danish AVestindia possessions. The Council was however of opinion, that it according to the whole nature of the matter, would be sufficient to address such a remonstrance to the Colonial Government. This petition, which the latter thought it but right to forward to the Ministry of Finances, in as much as it must be of interest for the Home Government to be made acquainted with the impression, which the question, that has been repeatedly urged in the mother country, about selling the colonies, has made upon the inhabitants of the islands and their representatives, is worded as follows : " The Council has received a proposition from the 3d member for the St. Thomas district, purporting that the same should approach His Majesty with a most submissive petition, containing a protest against the question, raised by some members of the Diet, regarding the sale of these colonies, which question has been taken up by a few of the Copenhagen electors, who have made it the subject of interpellations at the elections

for the last Diet. The Diet has rejected the proposition and the expressions on the subjeet which were heard at the elections, are to be considered as standing alone and isolated. The Colonial Council is in no way entitled to apprehend, that Bis Majesty or the Royal Government should entertain the slightest intention of proposing such a measure or, in case that the proposition should be repeated, of entering upon it. AAre are also firmly convinced, that no future Danish Government will ever reconcile itself to the idea of making about 40,000 men, who, with the exception of very few, have acquired the full right of Danish Burghers according to the qualifications required by the law and the rest of which have domiciled themselves and invested their capitals here with good confidence in the protection of the Danish laws and the Danish Government, an object of sale and transfer. AAre can the less reconcile ourselves to such an idea, as His Majesty in granting to the islands this consulting assembly, has expressly acknowledged the right of the inhabitants of passing their opinion on their own interests. The Council can thus merely repudiate the idea of a sale, whilst we would consider it hardly decent or becoming to address His Majesty with a formal remonstrance, an act which would in itself involve a doubt, that we have received no reason to entertain. The Council has therefore unanimously resolved, simply to express to His Majesty's representative, the Governor of these islands, the firm
hope and the unalterable conviction, which is in complete harmony with the sentiments of all the

s <D m <© i a a Ti s inhabitants ; that His Majesty would bo graciously pleased never to listen to such a proposition, in case it should at any time bo renewed. Colonial Council for the Danish AVestindia possessions, 30th November 1852. Kunzen, Chairman. Joiin H.Burt, Secretary. To the Government of the D. AV. possessions." After the Minister of Finances had most submissively laid the said petition before His Majesty the King in His Privy Council, His Majesty has been pleased, on the 3d June last, to resolve as follows : " AVe have most graciously caused this most submissive Report to be submitted to Us in Our Privy Council, and have with Royal pleasure taken notice of the national feeling and attachment to the Danish crown which are manifested in the declaration of the Colonial Council to Our Governor."

Lord I appeal to thee." The meanest capacity must be aware, that there is a natural propensity in man of self-preservation, prompting him to unite with his species, to guard against the dangers incident to life ; as also to devise effective means for the preservation of property. This is a self-evident truth admitted by all mankind, except a Arery-Ass. The scurrilous attack of "Veritas" (or more correctly þÿ Very- Ass) on the "voluntary principle," shows his utter ignorance of human nature, and exposes both his head and heart, proving plainly by his brayings, that he belongs to an inferior species, when he impertinently habitants of St. Thomas, " a curiosity" and its terms the petition of the most respectable Inmooter " unique." As nothing good can be expected from a 1'oul source, it is not surprising that, " A'eritas," should dure to calumniate and misunderstand the praise-worthy motives of the petitioners, or that he should endeavour to depreciate its author. He has certainly not profited by the march of intellect, nor by the correctives given him in the public papers, not long ago, wherein the animal was designated a liar," " and escaped chastisement in consequence of his cowardly incognito. It being the natural and mischievous propensities of his nature to annoy and disturb the peace of a community of which

lie is an unworthy member, it is his base object in his attack, of imputing to others, what so naturally belong to himself " iniquity and dastardliness." If this Assininc Individual had read the trite, but instructive fable of the old, but wise crow, which thought it time to decamp with her young, when the farmer resolved to cut down the grain himself and not depend on the promised assistance of his neighbors ; he might have understood the moral of the said petition : That a Brand Corps composed of men who have every thing to loose, will act promptly and effectively in case of fire. AVhereas Individuals forced by duty, to endanger their health and lives, cannot be expected to use the same energy. As the silly writer of the said article has had sufficient instinct to adopt an appropriate name, I am led to hope that it will not be lost labor, to endeavor to beat in the animal's brain, something like a correct knowledge of the subject he has had the temerity to meddle with. Otherwise it would be superfluous to add, what is already known by every man of sense in St. Thomas, and proved by the signatures of over 200 of the most respectable merchants and citizens : þÿ that the object of the address is not to undervalue the services of the Brand Corps at the last two fires, as many of its members deserve great praise for their exertions, but as a Body-Corporate þÿ it can-

not be denied, that the said Corps could be better organized in order that it may be more efficient The Island of St. Thomas, being the great emporium of trade in the AArest Indies, in consequence of the facilities, which her central position affords, has always an immense mass of property warehoused. No sane individual would therefore for a moment impute improper or ambitious motives to her princely and magnanimous merchants, for wisely adopting timely and effici ent means for the preservation of property, of which, we have precedence in all civilized countries. "Veritas' " appeal to "the impartial reader, every rational being, and every man, who has not taken a strong dose of self conceit, vanity and iniquity" will be laughed at. A'ice Admiral Baron do Lasusse whilst laying at Salamis with the fleet under his command, received despatches from Paris which contained the preremptory orders to proceed immediately to the Dardanelles ; be delayed his departure, desirous to communicate with the English admiral, and for that purpose despatched a steamer. Meanwhile Admiral Dundas sailed from Malta with his fleet, and after a short run of five days, anchored in the Bay of " Besika," exactly three days before the junction of the French fleet. On this intelligence reaching Paris, the Emperor ordered the immediate recall of Admiral Lasusse, and his removal to the list of the reserve, and the appointment of A'ice Admiral Hamlin to the command of the fleet, with orders to proceed immediately to the Bosphorus. The circumstance which apparently exhibits a disobedience of orders on the part of the French Admiral, is said to have caused considerable disappointment to the government, inasmuch that its activity had been in advance of the English, consequently its displeasure at the tardy movements of the French commander, and the sharpness with which it has manifested that displeasure. Another version of this affair is in circulation þÿ it is generally reported, that the French government, seized with eagerness the opportunity which enabled it, by the appointment of a junior Admiral, to gratify the amour propre of the British Nation, in the satisfaction of witnessing the allied fleets under the command of Admiral

Dundas, who according to naval etiquette, could not have aspired to that situation as long as Admiral Lasusse maintained his command ; the latter, by virtue of seniority, being entitled to the superior command in conformity with the regulations appertaining to the naval service. Admiral Hamlin is reputed, in the estimation of his colleagues, to be a great tactician ; perfectly qualified, by experience, with the duties of his profession, and possessing, to a remarkable degree, all the energy of character, and daring spirit, necessary to conduct or accomplish a great enterprize. He is the son of Admiral llamliu a gallant officer who died whilst in command of a French fleet occupied in the blockading of Gadiz at the time the Duke of Arigouletne entered into Spain at the head of a large army. Admiral Duperc was appointed as his successor, and had the good fortune to obtain after a few weeks service, the surrender of Cadiz by capitulation and moreover, the enjoyment of the honours of a triumph which would have devolved on his predecessor, without the event alluded. The greatest harmony and good feeling, is reported to exist among the commanders of the allied fleets in the Bay of Besika namely, Turk and Egyptian þÿ French and English, notwithstanding the concentration of a naval force unexampled in the annals of maritime history. The French and English governments have spontaneously organized a superior fleet already assembled and ready for sea at the first notice from a tele-

graphic despatch ; considering the peculiar nature of this naval force, ships of the liue with propellers. It is generally presumed, that the allied powers intend in the event of war to be prepared for a decisive demonstration in the Baltic and the natural consequence, the bombardment and destruction of CVonstadt. The St. Petersburg correspondent of the " London Times" announces that an army of 100,000 Russians with

all the equipments necessary to take the field was encamped along the river Pruth. And a subsequent communication distinctly states the fact, that orders had been given by the Emperor Nicolas for the immediate crossing of that river by his troops. Such movements evidently indicate war as inevitable, taking into consideration the declaration of the Emperor of the French to Mr. Kisseleff the Russian Ambassador ; " That the crossing of the Pruth would be considered by France (and which Mr. Kisseleff admitted) a casus bellis. It is also confirmed, that the Russian commanders had taken the precaution to obstruct the entrance of the Danube, by sinking a great number of boats loaded with ordnance ; by this manoeuvre, upwards of two hundred and fifty vessels with cargoes, ready for sea, have been in a manner, trapped and remain without being able to effect their egress The vast armaments of Russia; the activity of large bodies of troops, moving in all directions towards the frontiers ; the extensive orders despatched every where, for the accumulating of warlike stores and the purchase of an immense quantity of provisions, evidently point at a crisis indicative of the failure of all the resources of diplomacy, and the certainty of war ; a calamity which appears, beyond the power of human control : the more probable, in the presence of corresponding exertions on the part of the Turkish government, who with the most vigorous effects, and animated by natural enthusiasm, have organized such defences which, taken in connection

with the support of allies, enable it to look with confidence on the coming struggle. To taunt Russia, their inveterate and natural enemies ; and to turn a deaf ear to the counsels of those powers sincerely desirous of preventing a calamity which must, in the outset, involve every state in Europe, without any regard as to their position, gloomy aspects of European politics " the coming interest, or population. Such are the dark and events, which cast their shadows before them." We now turn towards that portion of the melancholy tableau r, which faintly offers the hope of a dispersion of the tempest. Among the powers who have in their anxiety despatched agents to the cabinet of the Sultan and the Czar; we notice the envoys of Spain - (tieneral Prim) Austria and England; these special agents will use their utmost exertions to avert the storm, and the failure of their mission, will be decisive of the result þÿ the opening of the Temple þÿ these movements indicate, the anxious desire of the parties to avoid the ultimaratin thus far, Austria and Prussia, have apparently maintained a neutral position ; by keeping aloof, from the wiles of diplomacy ; both powers being aware, that they have much to loose and little to gain by a continental war, have refrained from giving any pledge to either of the parties. Such is the position of two powers who cannot remain isolate on the breaking out of hostilities. On looking at France, we see the symptoms of those causes which explain the temper and moderation

shown by the Emperor in the presence of the vast hostile demonstration which we have already stated. The French police have succeeded in discovering a plot having for its object the assassination of the Emperor. In consequence of the discovery, a great number of persons have been arrested, but the official organs of the government continue silent, so that the ramifications are not in possession of the public : it is only known that sixty of the conspirators intended to attack the Emperor, whilst at the Hippodrome, whilst the others would have fired the different palaces. Notwithstanding the boldness of this conspiracy, the Emperor and Empress continued, as usual, to visit the public places. The latest intelligence from Paris via London, announces the probability cf an important change in the Cabinet, namely the withdrawal of the Minister of War, for the purpose of introducing to that post a minister whose sentiments are known to be in favour of the return of those generals who are at this moment in exile. An arrangement which, if carried into effect, will clearly demonstrate the intentions of the Emperor to be prepared for any emergency, by endeavouring to rally around his throne, men possessing great military qualities and whose services may be momently required by their country. Louis Napoleon having demanded from the Russian Emperor a distinct declaration whether he desired War or Peace, the greatest anxiety prevailed in Paris, to learn the reply which the Czar would return to that ener-

getic demand Meanwhile, considerable stress appears to have been laid on the contents of a letter received in Paris, from a correspondent occupying an important situation at the palace in St. " Petersburg. ft will be remembered tli;it by an extraordinary article in the Scnutns ConsuUum of the 7th of November, 1852, the Emperor reserved to himself power over the members of his own family, which placed them at his will, completely beyond the pale of law. Tn fact, so sweeping is the wording of the clause, the Emperor has power of life and death over them. Nojhing has since occurred to show that the occasion had arisen for exercising these powers, but this week the Mnni- Icur contains a decree, tilling several columns, in pursuance of the scnatus consullitm for the regulation of the imperial family. The decree con- ' litis amongst others the following provisions : þÿ Art. 1 The Emperor exercises over all the members of his family the rights of paternal power during their minority, and always prcrves with respect to them a power of surveillance and discipline. Art 3. The imperial family consists þÿ 1, of the legitimate or adopted descendants of the Emperor ; and 2, of the other princes called eventually to the succession by the Scnatus Consultuin of the 17th November, 1852, of their wives and legitimate children. Art. 1. The marriage of members of the imperial family, at whatever age they may be, shall be null of full right and without there being any need of judgment, whenever it may have been contracted without the formal consent of the Emperor. Art. 5. All children born of a union which shall not have been contracted in conformity with the preceding article, shall be considered illegiti-

mate. Art. ti. The matrimonial conventions of members of the imperial family shall be null, if not approved by of the Emperor ; without, in that case, the parties being entitled to appeal to the enactments of the Code Napoleon. For llic M|. Croix Avid. the voluntary principle. The most dreadful of all conceivable calamities is the belief of having discovered a new and popular theory. The piece of transcendentalism which has struck the mooter of the petition like a coup notion, that whereas what he calls voluntary ile solid proves sufficiently the proposition. The " principle" ought to obtain universally with all

® WW tA am % A 4?2 S men sympathy and co-operation þÿ so there ought to exist uo plan, no system nor clue to guide them out of the labyrinth into which he attempts to inveigle them þÿ appears to be a fancy which may render a sensitive mind miserable for life. An ill digested petition is got up ostensibly for the purpose of abolishing the established Brand Corps and to put in its place a voluntary Company of Firemen is in a " state of disorganization." The fines and ? Why ? Because the Brandcorps imprisonment prescribed by the Militia Law arc not stringent enough to force men to do their duty, and thus by a kind of reasoning which cannot pass current among men in a sound state of mind, the w he arrives at the conclusion, that it ought ' to be entirely left to the tender conscience of men to perform a duty the most ungrateful and dangerous, involving the loss of health and life ! The notion is ridiculous þÿ ther the writer's " celebral activity" has been nay, it is sublimely so. Eistunted in its development by a mass of projects, which luckily for this community have always proved to be vapours and bubbles as extravagant as ever have been produced by an overheated imagination, or there is a want of candour and it sincerity in his coming out on the public ; for is certain, that he could not otherwise have failed so signally in tracing out the evil to its proper source. We admit that there are many evils to be remedied ; we admit, that the Brandcorps ought to be reorganized ; but it is owing to other

reasons than those adduced by the writer of the petition. It is not our province to exhaust the subject, nay, we do not feel ourselves capable of doing so. But the following reasons appear there- to be among many others forcible, and we to us fore set them forth : 1 , The organization of the Brandcorps as it now exists is not suitable to the spirit of the age. The line of demarcation between 1st division and 2d division ought to be abolished as soon as possible ; in short a perfect amalgamation ought to take place forthwith. 2, The burden which now rests exclusively on the members of the Brandcorps ought to be transferred equally on the shoulders of the members of the other Militia corps. In fact, as long as we have a strong military force garrisoned here, we can dispense with the armed militia þÿ the members of which ought to be converted into firemen. There can be no doubt that the signers of the petition, will voluntarily enroll themselves in the Fire Company at once. It cannot be expected, that þÿ -in the language of the Scripture þÿ they will bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders ; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers. 3, The commander of the Brandcorps ought invariably to be a practical man, one whose daily occupation renders him familiar with the use of engines, bills, and axes. We do not intend by this proposal to reflect disrespectfully on the conduet of the theoretical men who hitherto have

been chiefs of the Brandcorps. Far from it. We, on the contrary ; wish that the practical men may be attended with the good luck at least of the theoretical chief of the Brandcorps now absent. These are the principles we subscribe to, and we believe every honest man will do so likewise. And when we find the author of the petition advocating these principles, we shall readily give him more credit for sincerity and candour in regard to the bona fide object of his new principle, han with respect to the cause which is said by him to have rendered it necessary St Thomas, 22nd July, 1853. Canvass Town. þÿ Canvass Town (as the name implies) is a town of tents ; it is on the southern side of the Yaira, and about a quarter of a mile distant from Melbourne. At the time I write llieie arc between GOO and 700 tents þÿ perhaps more, and the population amounts to 5,000 or G 000 souls. 1 lie tents are ananged in rows more or less regular, and with a squalid pleasantry some ol them have been called after certain well-known streets in England þÿ Urgent-street, Bondstreet, Liverpool-street ; while many of the tents have assumed ostentatious titles of distinction. We have the London Cotlee-rooms, the Euiopcan Dining-rooms, the Great Britain Stores, the Isle of Wight lent, the Golden Lion Stores (such a lion !), the National Dining-rooms and Lodging-tent, Dover Clill, LI Dorado, the Coflee and 1 ea-coke Depot. There are tailors, butchers, bakers, shoemakers, ironmongers, blacksmiths, hard-ware and crockery-stalls, tinmen Almost every tent exhibits slops, books, cabin furniture or utensils, with other articles of which the owners have no need here. Neatly every second tent also sells ginger-beer or letniu nde. There ate two physicians' tents, who of course arc at the same time surgeons, den-
tists, corn-cutters, and apothecaries. Young gentlemen of family and education drive

off in the bush) ; and oh, ye classic groves, where the trees have fresh green leaves þÿ of which there are no signs here in summer þÿ how many University men does this strange collection of tents, with all their gipsy hie appurtenances, contain? There are several besides myself; and some ladies also, besides my wife. It took me some days to learn these particulars j but how many days would it take to ascertain the amount of disappointment, privation, and misery which these iraii walls conceal from view ? The general appearance of this unique town is not very easy to describe It lias too many tents to he at all like a gipsy encampment, and the utter want of all uniformity in the tents renders it quite as unlike an Arab settlement or military encampment. The nearest thing of all to it is that of a prodigiously extensive þÿfair all tents and small booths, but without shows music, games, visitors, or an) thing pleasant It has no gilt, and very little gingerbread Luxury, of the most cheap and childish kind has no place here ; even comfort, partly lor want of money, but more on account of dust, is impossible. Finally, there is a mixture ol the highly educated with the totally uneducated, the refined with the semi-brutal (many a convict with his bulldog being among us), all dressing as roughly and faring precisely alike. There are several sects of religion here, and on Sunday the air is filled with tic voices of the praying and singing of thes, different persuasions, all going on at the

same lime at different parts of the gn und and all in some degree audible to an impar tial listener in his own tent. There are new tents of waterproof canvas, "best twice boiled navy brown," number one canvas, number two, three, four, down to brown ho'land and bleached or unbieachcd calico There arc blue tents, bed-tick tents, and wain-covered waggons. There are square0 and rounds, and triangles and wedges, and pyramids, frame- works ol rough branches and tents like tall sugarloavos or extinguishers, and others of the squab molehill form, and many of no definite form, being in some instances double and triple (one tent opening it-side into another), and in other instances having been blown all awav by the winds, or set up badly, or witli rotten cordage Here and there you sec patchwork tents, made up of all sorts of odds and ends of bedding, clothing, blankets, sheets, aprons, petticoats, and counterpanes, or old sails and pieces of tarpaulin, matting, packing stuff, and old bits of board with the tin linining ol a case of goods, old bits of linen of all colours filling up the intervals. Sometimes, also, you come upon a very melancholy one which makes you þÿpause a so-called tent of six leet long, rising from a slant to three feet high in the middle, so small and low indeed that the wretched occupant (with perhaps, a wife) must crawl in beneath it like a dog, and lie there till he crawls out again. It is like a squalid tumulus þÿ Dickens' Household Words

To the Editor of the þÿ þÿTidcndc. þÿSir, Having read in your paper of the 17th instant, an article copied from the Saint Christopher Gazette, wherein the events in the Island of Tortola are professed to be detailed from information obtained from a þÿ recent þÿarrival via this Island, and also a comment on the conduct of certain of the officials, not warranted by facts, and we are compelled to say under the circumstances of the case, exceedingly ungenerous and detail unmanly. We beg to furnish you and an account of the Insurrection in the exciting causes, as far as the same shall be admissible, pending the legal investigation which is now proceeding in the Island of Tortola, anti the conduct of those officials, during and subsequent to the outbreak on the first and second instant, and to the present time, from a review of which the Editor of the Gazette will, we doubt not, regret his unjust animadversions and mistimed pleasantry. Some time past the Legislature of Tortola finding it impossible in the then state of the Island, to raise sufficient means by taxation for the exigencies of the Colony, particularly for the support of the poor, the prisoners in gaol, and the repairs of the court house, and other public buildings, they requested a loan from the British Government. This aid was refused, and it was urged by the Executive that some further means of taxation should be devised. In accordance with this recommendation, the Legislature, amongst other matters, imposed an additional tax of þÿsix-p ence a-

head on cattle. As a great part of this property belonged to the emancipated classes they expressed a disinclination to submit to it, and this disinclination proceeded to a determination on their part not to pay; þÿ it is supposed they were partially excited to this opposition, by a meeting held on the twenty-fourth of May last, at the Wesleyan Chapel. The Honorable John James Haddock, a member of Council, and a local preacher, in the chair. What the language made use of at that meeting was, the writer is not prepared to state, but the negroes left with the impression that the petition, then got up, was for the purpose of exempting the members of the Wesleyan Society from all taxation whatsoever. About this time, Mr. Augustus Me Ci.everty called on Mr. Thomas William Crooke, one of Her þÿMajesty Jus- s tices of the Peace, and told him that the country people were desirous of getting off the contemplated additional tax on cattle ; in consequence of which, Mr. Crooke rode out with Mr. McCleverty, to a place called Chateau Belle Air, and there he met several people whom he recommended to memorialize the Legislature against this tax, but as there were not sufficient persons then present, the meeting was adjourned to another day. On that day Mr. Crooke attended in company with Mr. McCleverty, and a great many persons had assembled, but as the majority appeared to think this memorial would interfere with the one sent forward by the Methodist Missionaries, he refused to have anything

further to do with the matter. These circumstances are detailed with a view of shewing how exceedingly dangerous it is to address or agitate such persons on political subjects. We shall leave the Methodist Ministers to their own reflections, and hope their explanation will be such as to remove the obloquy that must necessarily rest on them in

the present excited state of the public mind. As to Mr. Justice Crooke, his houses have been burned down þÿ and he with his family, are now amongst the destitute refugees in this Island. The cattle-tax was payable at the Treasury, from the first to the tenth day of this month. On the first, numbers of negroes arrived from the country, nearly all armed with bludgeons, and proceeded directly to the Treasuþÿrer Office, s where it appeared they made a great clamour, and some of them tendered to the Treasurer the former tax of one shilling, which he stated he could not receive þÿ t Hat he must act according to law þÿ and could not receive less than one shilling and six-pence. This was also explained to them by the Chief Justice, and Mr. William Henry Shew, and other officials; but the party became more clamorous. It was deemed necessary to arrest one of the individuals, and he was taken before Mr. Justice Pringle, by whom he was convicted under the good order and decorum Act, and fined £ 1 , and in default, imprisonment. Whilst taking this man to prison an attempt was made at rescue, but the constables (one of whom was knocked down, and the other lost the writ of commitment), succeeded ultimately in lodging the prisoner in gaol, and in capturing one of the persons attempting the rescue. Mr Justice Shew proclaimed the Riot Act, and the before mentioned functionaries endeavored to quiet the people and to point out the danger of resisting the laws, but without effect; however

the constables, a number of special ones having been sworn in, succeeded in lodging the second offender in gaol ; in doing so, they were attacked with sticks and stones. The Colonial Secretary was severely cut in the head and several of the constables wounded, but continued to use their staves with some effect. The rioters ultimately left the town using threats that they would þÿ next day in greater numbers pull down return the the gaol þÿ lire the town þÿ and destroy the white and coloured inhabitants. The officials then waited on His Honor the President, and recommending him to proclaim Martial Law, and to send off to the authorities of this island for aid. The President declined to proclaim Martial Law, however he directed Mr. Justice Shew to take muskets out of the Arsenal, and arm the special constables þÿ and to purchase for the Government all the powder in the town : this was done arid a proclamation was issued, ordering all Rum Slio'ps to lie closed. A patrole was appointed for the town, a the court house in the cellar of which, guard placed at þÿ the gaol, and another at the arms were deposited, and a messenger sent off to St. Thomas with the Preþÿsident s despatch, but the authorities here not supposing the danger so imminent, as it afterwards proved, that promptness which has been heretofore evinced by the Danish authorities, was not observed, but so soon as the real state of affairs was known a detachment of Troops was sent off. On Tuesday, the second instant, the

country negroes arrived in town in great numbers, and were joined by the disaffected about town ; they commenced their clamours as before at the Treasuþÿrer Office, s and their threats were most violent and alarming. The Chief Justice proclaimed the Riot Act, and himself and Mr. Justice Haddock both addressed the mob in a manner calculated to conciliate and appease them. They demanded the release of the two men who had been imprisoned the day before, which was acceded to by the President when the mob proceeded to the gaol,

soon after returning and congregated opposite the Chief þÿJustice house, s then the residence of Mr. Wm. H. Shew, where a part of the constables was assembled, the Magistrates again proclaimed the Riot Act, and advised the mob to return peaceably to their homes, but no notice was taken ofthem, and when the words þÿ God save the þÿQueen were uttered, the most horrid and treasonable 'expressions time At this were used by the mob. This þÿ but they persisted they were and at impossible, told was length commenced stoning the house, both in front and rear, wounding some of the inmates, breaking all the windows and some ot the furniture, when a few shots were fired, more for the purpose of intimidating the rioters, but the attack and threats became more violent, and in self defence, the constables and others in the house were compelled to fire with deadly aim, when one man was killed and many wounded.

I Dwellings for tlie Poor in Paris The Paris correspondent of the London Times, writing on Tuesday, says : þÿ 1 am assured that there are two projects of decrees now before the Emperor, to one of which very probably the imperial signature has been by this time affixed. They both relate to a subject which will excite no small interest, and may perhaps please one class of citizens, but will dissatisfy another. The object ol one of these projects is to authorise the formation of a company for tbe construction on an immense scale of lodginghouses for the operative classes. The company, 1 am told, will be guaranteed 4i per cent, on their outlay, but the administration. that is the Government, will have the power to fix the maximum ofthe rent to he charged for the rooms. For a þÿnight lodging s and a single room, 20 centimes, or 4 sous, will be the maximum. These immense buildings are to be erected in the finest and healthiest quarters of Paris, in the immediate, They neighbourhood of the with will be furnished railroad termini wash-hous es, bathing places, gardens, walks, &e., and otherwise provided with every comfort suited to the class for which they are intended, and to whom the apart inents will be let out, furnished or un furnished, at a moderate rent. A similar undertaking for the accommodation and comfort of tbe subaltern employes Government offices, and the of petits rentiers, whose means The is also to be entered upon. arc limited, healthiest spots will be selected for these buildof gardens, baths, ings, and they will have other and the advantage comforts ;

it is even said that eating-houses will be comprised. Here also a certain amount John Davies the first Revenue Officer, I of interest will be guaranteed ; but, as in the former case, the Government will have tbe power of fixing the maximum of rent to be charged. These projects have, however, a touch of Socialism in them ; and, so far as the internal arrangements are concerned, these vast establishments will bear a striking resemblance to the Phalansterian system. The proprietors of houses will, there is little doubt, be much dissatisfied at the prospect of so formula hie an opposition, and it is not certain whether the workmen will be content. They already say they are under sufficient discipline during the day in their workshops, without again submitting to it after their work is at. an end ; and they will, very probably, look upon these establishments as so many huge places of confinement, where they will be eternally under the eye of the certain that the poorer classes police. It suf- is have fered a great deal from the vast improvements that have been going on, and are still going on, in Paris, and precisely in the quarters inhabited by these classes. Those narrow and filthy streets, with

over-crowdeil and unwholesome houses, are being swept away, and it is calculated that already not less than 1500 houses have been levelled to the ground in those parts of the city. The consequence is that the working men, who were the principal tenants, have been obliged to move elsewhere, and the disappearance of such a mass of buildings has had the effect of raising to an exorbitant degree house rent in every quarter of Paris. Perhaps the proprietors of houses have too eagerly availed themselves of the necessities of a considerable part of the population ; it is certain that house rent has, in many instances, increased full '50 per cent', within the last few months. However that may be, lam assured that the Emperor, who has been long engaged in the study of the projects in question, is determined on authorising the companies alluded to.

TAKE TIMS JOHN. ADVICE OF AN OLD I.ADY. Now, John, listen to me for I am older than you, or 1 could not be your mother. Never do you marry a young woman, John, before you have contrived to happen to be at the bouse where she lives, at least four or five times before breakfast. You should know bow late she lies in bed in the morning. You should take notice whether her complexion is the same in the morning as it is in the evening, or whether the morning wash and the towel have robbed her of her evening bloom. You should take care to surprise her, so that you may see her in her morning dress, and observe how her hair looks, when she is not expecting you. You should hear the morning conversation between her and her mother. If she is ill-natured and snappish to her mother, so she will be to you, depend upon it. But if you find her up and neatly dressed in the morn in" with the same countenance, the same smiles, the same neatly combed hair, the same ready and pleasant answers to her mother, which characterised her appearance and deportment in the evening, and particularly if she is lending a band to get the breakfast ready in good season þÿ she is a prize, John, and the you secure her to yourself the better.

THE NEGRO: AN INCIDENT IN HEAD LIFE. One winter evening, when norland winds were piping, loudly, but harmlessly around the yvalls of our old substantial English dwelling, our whole family, consisting of four persons þÿ namely, my father and mother, my sister and þÿmyself were sitting before a cheerful fire, enjoying that dim delicious hour that intervenes between the night and the day, ere shutters are closed, or candles placed on the table. On the present occasion, this hour was spun out to an unusual length, and yet not one of us felt inclined to have the lights brought in. My father, who had been much abroad during his life, was peculiarly animated in his narration of the various scenes he had witnessed, and our questions ever and anon stimulated him to some fresh recollection. A pause at last ensued, however ; and the close of the twilight enjoyment seemed inevitable, when my sister put a question which prolonged it lor a considerable time further. þÿ What, said she, þÿ wasthe happiest passage lather, in your life V 14 less her dear heart! had the candles been Haring upon the table, she would not have put that question. She was then eighteen, and the blissful dream of love was uppermost in her thoughts. Hut my þÿfather reply s had no reference to that subject, as the reader will learn, it he has patience enough to peruse the following story, as it came from the narþÿrator lips s : þÿ I shall tell you. my þÿchildren, said our father, þÿ what passage in my life

gives me most satisfaction in the retrospect. Soon after your mother had united her fate with mine, I fell into a respectable and profitable business in New York, where, as you are aware, that competency was earned which now enables me to pass the evening of life in comfort in my native England. The occupation which 1 followed required my daily presence for some hours in the centre of that city, where 1 met the parties with whom I had business connections. The time which I generally chose for this purpose was the hottest part of the day, when every one almost is within doors, and there was less chance of missing my object. The streets at this period of the day are often remarkably empty, only a straggler being visible here and there. It was on one of these business visits that I saw, in a back-street, two men, an Irishman and a negro, jostling, or rather struggling with each other. There was no other object in the street to divert my attention, and I therefore almost involuntarily kept my eyes fixed upon the men. The negro was a powerful, athletic man, and had evidently the better in the struggle, which speedily became a complete wrestle. The Irishman felt his inferiority, and, becoming irritated, raised his arm, and gave his opponent a tremendous blow, which felled him to his knees. The Irishman after this threw himself into a defensive attitude, and on the black raising himself from the ground, blows were rapidly interchanged by the parties. All this passed almost instanta-

neously, and the issue was equally speedy. The negro struck his adversary on the side of the head with sufficient force to drive linn to the ground. The unfortunate Irishman's head came in contact with a stone, and his skull was fractured. W ithin a few moments after the fall, lie was dead ! 1 No one was near enough to witness the course ol this affair but myself. A crowd, however, soon collected on the spot; and as the street was chiefly inhabited by the labouring Irish, the assemblage was principally composed of

8W« WiU A NT 1 a that nation. The wounded man was carried into a house to receive medical assistance, and I, losing sight of the negro, proceeded on my way home. þÿ My own affairs occupied so much of þÿit. my time and attention, that the unhappy incident I had witnessed passed almost entirely from my mind. A few mornings after it happened, however, I was much shocked to perceive by the newspapers, that the negro had been committed to prison on a charge of wilful murder, several Irishmen having sworn before the coroner, that they had seen the black strike the deceased with a stone. To give colour to this assertion, one of them had the audacity to bring forward what the newspapers called þÿ the fatal þÿstone. Horrified at such villainy as this, I instantly formed the resolution of going forward at the trial, and telling the truth as I had witnessed it. Your mother and my friends attempted in vain to dissuade me, on the ground that I would inevitably incur, by such conduct, the hatred of the lower orders of the Irish, who, disappointed of their victim, might wreak their revenge on me. A sense of duty to the negro and to justice enabled me, thank Heaven, to resist these representations, though reason admitted their feasibility. þÿ The poor þÿgers, negro is, like myself, said I; þÿ he is far in a land of stran- from the hearth of his infancy, and perhaps has not one friend in the world. He is of a persecuted and despised race; and, come what may, 1 am resolved that he shall at least have the advantage of having the truth

stated regarding the melancholy accident in which lie has been þÿinvolved. Itecollcct, my children, that this was only my duty, and that the peculiar circumstances of the case alone gave my resolve þÿ if, indeed, it did possess þÿ any merit. þÿ On the morning of the trial, I was in attendance at the court-house. On applying for admittance to the grand juryroom, I was informed that a true bill had been found against the negro, and that the gentlemen on the jury had given orders for the admission of no more witnesses, being perfectly satisfied with the evidence laid before them. I was not to he put off, however, in this manner, hut forced my way, almost in spite of the attending official, into the room, and after relating the whole of my story to the grand jury, was admitted as an evidence. At the same time, the true bill already found was held still as the conclusion to which these gentlemen had come, and the poor þÿnegro life s was thus left dependent on the effect of my testimony at the trial. þÿ The case came on. Witness after witness swore to the same facts, until the jury were thoroughly satisfied, and the court impatient to hear the sentence pronounced against a wretch so vile as the black seemed to be. 11c, poor fellow, seemed more thunder-struck at the deliberate falsehoods uttered, than alarmed at his dangerous predicament. No voice was lifted up in his favour; no eye glanced on him with compassion or sympathy ; friendless and hopeless, he sat like a being of an inferior kind among

his fellow-men. I was called at length, and gave a plain and full statement of the facts of the case : þÿ That I was the only person in the street, besides the deceased and the prisoner, at the time of the occurrence ; that I knew neither of the parties; that the Irishman struck the negro first, bringing him on his knees with the blow, and causing the blood to gush from his nose; that the black rose, and wiping the blood from his face with his left hand, after a short struggle, with the same hand gave the Irishman a blow on the side of the head, which drove
him to the ground, where his head, striking the curb-stone, was fatally injured ; and that no stone could possibly be in the þÿnegro s hand without my observing

þÿ I feel pleasure, my children, in stating, for the honour of human nature, that a buzz of satisfaction ran through the couft-room at the conclusion of my story. My own character and station in life, together with the total absence of interested motives, caused the entire overthrow of the previous evidence, and compassion and sympathy for the accused took the place of anger and abhorrence in every breast. The counsel for the prosecution alone, as was natural perhaps, acted as if unsatisfied. He cross-examined me very closely, and made me repeat so often the manner in which the negro struck the deceased, and with which hand he did it, that my patience became in the end exhausted, and 1 brought matters to a conclusion by suiting the action to the word, and applying my fist pretty smartly to the side of his own head. The solemnity of the occasion could not restrain the laughter that broke forth, and the barrister sat down, satisfied, it appeared at length, and somewhat chop-fallen. The jury, without the slightest hesitation, acquitted the prisoner of the charge of murder, and returned a verdict of manslaughter. lie was sentenced to be imprisoned for some months ; but this was merely formal, for in a few days lie was restored to perfect þÿliberty. þÿ Hid you ever hear of the negro af þÿterwards? interrupted iny sister. þÿ never I saw him more than two or three times. The first time was about a month after the trial, when, in passing an oyster-shop or cellar, a voice called

out: þÿ Massa G ! Massa G þÿ! I turned, and recognised in the owner of the store the unfortunate negro. His gratitude for the service which accident had enabled me to do tor him, was writ ten in every line of his countenance. He compelled me lo taste a few of his oysters, and anxiously pressed me lo inform him of my residence, that he might carry thither present þÿ when me stand at bar without friend, for me. þÿ Ah, his whole stock as a þÿmassa, said lie, and when me saw þÿ pectable gentleman go in box, me tink, what ! you going to hang me too! Hut when me heard mas sa speak true, me tank God for sending one gentleman to speak my cause. De blessing will be answered from dc sky which poor nigger speak for Massa G . Me could not help cry de first time many þÿyear. And the tears again ran down his cheeks as he spoke. þÿ This passage of my þÿlife, continued my father, if not the happiest at the þÿ time, is at least one of the most pleasing to look back upon. And this, my children, is the best test of all happy passages in þÿlife. þÿ Did you suffer nothing for your behaviour from those wretches of Irishmen V asked my sister þÿ þÿ those vindicþÿtive þÿ þÿ Hush, þÿBetsy, said my father; þÿ do not vent general reflections, as I fear you were about to do, upon a nation which has shewn so many great and good men in the list of her sons, and whose every error has been owing to ignorance, and, it may be, hard usage. Those Irishmen who were connected with the affair I have described, were

The screams of the poor creature at the lastmentioned operation were the cause, that his attention was attracted, and on giving the unfeeling wretch a severe rebuke he was received with a laugh. Upon inquiry as to this abominable practice be has been told, that it is quite customary among the half-savages here, in order to get what they call live feathers, to pick before killing, guinea-birds, turkeys, geese, etc., nay even to stick pegs through their j heads, causing them a lingering agony, on pretence that their meat is improving thereby. Such atrocities ought to be looked after and to be prevented, as the killing of a poor animal for our use is quite enough to show the superior right of man without at the J same time torturing it. This is not written for the sake of the menials ; but such of their betters, as do not equal them in callousness, may perhaps take some notice of these lines to prevent the continuation of these barbarities.' j Comforts of an Editor þÿ If be does not fill bis sheet with news of iuiportauce, whether there is any or not, it is condemned for not being what it purport to be þÿ a newspaper. If be does not fill at least one column every week with something laughable, bis folio is pronounced uninteresting. First use of Gas as an Artificial Light . þÿ In the year 1792, Mr. Murdoch made use of gas in lighting his house and office at Redruth, in Cornwall, where he then resided. The mines at which he worked being distant some miles from his house, he was in the constant practice of filling a bladder with coal-gas, in the neck of which he fixed a metallic tube, with a small orifice, through which the gas issued ; this being ignited, served as a lantern to his way for the considerable distance lie had nightly to traverse. This mode of illumination being then generally unknown if was thought by the common people that magical art alone could produce an effect. þÿ Clegg's Treatise on Coal-gas

For the last few evenings a Comet has been observed in the Western part of the Heavens, about 20 or 25 degrees above the horizon. This mysterious " visitor" can be distinctly seen between 7 and 8 o'clock in the evening. It has also been visible abroad as we learn

" There has been a Comet visible to us since the evening of the 22nd instant; it has a tail of about 9 or 10 degrees long. I have not yet heard l'hilologus' opinion on the erratic stranger." Below we publish a description of Comets, copied from Comstock's System of Natural Philosophy: COMETS. " Besides the planets which move round the sun in regular order, and in nearly circular orbits, there belongs to the solar system an unknown number of bodies called Comets, which move round the sun in orbits exceedingly eccentric, or elliptical, and whose appearance among our heavenly bodies is only occasional. Comets, to the naked eye, have no visible disc, but shine with a faint glimmering light, and arc accompanied by a train or tail, turned from the sun, and which is sometimes of immense length. They appear in every region of the heavens, and move in every possible direction. "Comets have been considered the harbingers of war, pestilence, or some other great or general evil ; and it was not until astronomy had made considerable progress as a science, that these strangers could be seen among our planets without the expectation of some direful event. " It had been supposed that Comets moved in straight lines, coming from the regions of infinite, or unknown space, and merely passing by our system, on their way to regions equally unknown and infinite, and from which they never returned. Sir Isaac Newton was the first to demonstrate that Comets pass round the Sun, like the planets, hut that

their orbits are exceedingly elliptical, and extend out to a vast distance beyond the solar system. "The number of Comets is unknown, though some Astronomers suppose that there are nearly 590 belonging to our system. "Of these, however, there are only three whose periods of return among us are known with any degree of certainty. The first of these has a period of 75 years; the second a period of 129 years; and the third a period of 575 years. The third appeared in 1980, and therefore cannot lie expected again until the year 2225. This Comet, iri 1(580, excited the most intense interest among the Astronomers of Europe, on account of its great apparent size, and near approach to our system. In the most remote part of its orbit, its distance from the sun was estimated at about eleven thousand two hundred millions of miles (1 1,200,000,000.) My lords, þÿ seeing the noble lord (Lord Clarendon) in his place, I rise to put a question with re? pec t to a report lately received from the Bauubian provinces of Wallachia and Moldavia From accounts, in the newspapers it appears that the military authorities of Russia in that country bad taken entire military possession, and had proceeded to administer the internal affairs of those provinces. It is said that the Russian coramandcr-in-chicf has ordered the Hospodars not to pay any tribute to the Porte ; and it is further stated in one report that the Russian Consul general went so far as to say that any tribute paid by the Hospodars to the Sultan would have to bo paid over again to his own master. It is moreover stated that those persons to whom were entrusted the administration of the country, were ordered to hold no further communication with Turkey. This, my lords, is a virtual and a real assumption of sovereignty over those principalities. It is impossible, my lords, that such an act can take place without leading directly to a terrible war þÿ (hear, hear). It is right, therefore, that this House and the country should have all the information the government can afford, without delay, and at the earliest possible period. This, my lords, is a matter of the gravest and deepest importance, and 1 hold it to be impossible for not only Europe, but France and England, to submit to such an extension of territory in that direction by Russia, or such a diminution of the

Turkish Empire, without the gravest and most fearful consequences. The matter, my lords, is of the greatest importance, not merely as regards the political balance of Europe and the honour of those countries who have guaranteed by treaty the integrity of the Turkish empire, but as regards the material interests of all persons in France, Germany, and especially in England þÿ (hear). It is therefore a matter on which all must be desirous of having the fullest intbrmation that, with propriety, can be given, and I hope my noble friend will not think me indiscreet if 1 ask if any such reports have reached him officially, and whether he can inform the House how far it is true that the assumption of the sovereignty of the Danubiuu provinces by Russia has taken place f The Earl of Clarendon. þÿ My lords, so far from thinking my noble friend has committed an indiscretion in the question lie has put to me, 1 beg to state I take the same view ho does as to the result, not only to Turkey, but to Europe, and especially this country, if we permit or allow the alienation of the Danubiau territories from the Turkish empire. I am, therefore, glad the noble lord has put the question to me thus early, that the public mind may bo satisfied by my giving my noble friend all the information I possess. By a despatch dated the 17th of July, I learned from Lord Stratford de Rcdcliffe, that a communication had been made by the consul general of Russia to the llospodar of Moldavia, informing him that his relations with the Turkish govern-
ment, on the ground, as stated, that although there existed no intention to modify the internal

institutions of Moldavia, or of altering the existing order of things, yet during the military occupation of the provinces acts of sovereign power on the part of Turkey must be necessarily, though temporarily, suspended I may state also, that the Turkish government have received similar information relative to the Ilospodar of Walla chia ; but a dispatch has been received from Mr. Combe, the consul general at Bucharest, dated the 22nd of last month, in which it was stated, up to that time no such communication had been made to the Hospodar of Wallachia. Such a communication to Wallachia, was, however, naturally expected by the Porte as that which had been made to Moldavia. These acts had determined the Porto to order the Ilospodars to withdraw from the provinces and to cease their offices Mr. Combe's dispatch added, that in such an event lie should consider it highly improper for tlic British consuls in the principalities to continue to exercise their functions there. My lords, on the receipt of this dispatch I lost no time in communicating to Lord Stratford dc Redcliffo the entire approval of her Majesty's government of his intentions þÿ (hear, hear). I can only, for the further information of your Lordships, say that I shall this evening forward advices by special messenger to Sir Hamilton Seymour to demand from the Russian government that explanation to which wc are entitled with respect to proceedings which T look at in the same light as my noblo friend þÿ (hear, hear).
