Mr Editor, þÿ Until within the last four or live years, an opinion very generally prevailed that those industrious and frugal persons who deposited whatever spare money they had iu a savings bank had, what is commonly termed, " Government security," for the return of their deposits, with interest ; in short, that they had the same security as parties who invested their money in ilte Three per Cent. Consuls, or any other Government stock. The failure of, and consequent stoppage in 1849, of several savings banks in Ireland, through the fraudulent conduct of the parties to whom their management was entrusted, dispelled this illusion. When the Government of that day was called upon to make good the money of which the depositors in these banks had been robbed, all liability on their part out denied. Tn vain it was pointed was distinctly that these establishments were, to a certain extent, placed under the control of the Government, by various Acts of Parliament, passed for the better regulation of savings hanks. The answer was brief, but conclusive, " There is not a clause in any one of those Acts that renders the Government in any way responsible for the payment of money that has been deposited in savings banks." The Government appointed a select committee to report upon the circumstances connected with the failure of certain savings hanks in Ireland. Other inquiries were made with reference to savings banks in this country, and the result proved that it was the paramount duty of the Government to

place these excellent institutions on a more satisfactory footing. Previous to which, however, as a matter of course, the usual number of papers, returns, were moved for and obtaimffl, ineluding that of the number of savings banks that had failed, and the loss the depositors had thereby sustained. At length, when, with all the necessary evidence before them, the Legislature could no longer delay bringing forward a measure which would give to the most deserving class of her Majesty's subjects every possible encouragement to habits of industry and frugality, and at the same time, afford them complete sceurity for the safety and due return of the amount

® Ui <0 S 2C A W I 8 they had deposited in the establishments appointed under the express sanction of the Government for the reception thereof, a Rill has been prepared by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, jointly with Mr. Bouverie and Mr. Wilson, to amend the laws relating to savings banks, and, in certain eases, to give the guarantee of the Government, to the depositors for the repayment of the sums legally deposited in such savings banks. That. Bill was printed on Wednesday last ; and I need scarcely inform your readers that, so great was the anxiety of the immense number ot persons interested in this important question to know what were the principal features of the Government Bill for the future regulation of savings banks, that orders were forwarded from all parts of the couutry to obtain copies of it as early as possible, and that, iu of consequence, number was disposed as soou as issued. With the whole these preliminary remarks, I have now to request their attention to some of the most important provisions of this interesting measure. Before doinn' so, I may, perhaps, be allowed to state that the preamble is much longer than the introductory part of ordinary Bills, and is to the following effect : þÿ That numerous banks for savings have been established under the authority of the Acts now in force in that respect for the safe custody and increase of small savings belonging to tlie industrious classes of her Majesty's subjects, and it is expedient to give further security to depositors

in such banks, and afford additional facilities for depositing such make that purpose to savings in safe custody, and for further provision respecting the same, and give additional powers to the Commissioners for the reduction of the National l>ebt, for the establishment of other savings banks, and the due regulation of those existing, so as to ensure to all depositors in savings banks, whether established before or subsequent to the passing of this Act, that they shall be duly repaid all moneys legally deposited with them, and interest thereon' It then provides that the Commissioners may authorize the establishment of savings banks in all cases where the parties proposing to manage them are willing to become jointly and severally personally responsible to depositors therein, or are desirous that a receiver, to the receive and pay deposits, shall be appointed by Commissioners. Such authority shall be signified in | writing, notice of which shall be it given don Gazette, in which notice shall bo stated in the Lonwhether such bank is established, with the guarantee of the Government, on the responsibility of the trustees and managers to depositors therein, and then provides, that when the receiver is appointed by the commissioners, the depositors in such bank shall have the guarantee of the Government for repayment to them of all sums deposited, <$-c., together with interest due thereon; but where the receiver is not appointed by the commissioners the trustees and managers shall be

jointly and severally responsible to the depositors. A list of their names, residences, etc., is to be forwarded to the commissioners, and every change by death or otherwise certified to them. It will be seen that in either ease, whether the Government appoints the receiver or not, the depositors will in future have a greater security tor the proper carc and due return of their money, with the interest due thereon, than ever they possessed hitherto, even with reference to the best conducted of these institutions ; but I apprehend that the majority of the depositors of the savings banks will prefer the plan by which their investments will be placed under Government security to that of the responsibility of mere trustees, however I respectable tliey may be. of The Act iurtlicr vides that, if the trustees any savings bank al- proready established shall of positors the guarantee Government desire to obtain tor the de- for the repayment of their deposits, but without the appointment of a receiver by the commissioners, and shall within three months after the passing of the Act, signify under their hands and seals their willingness to make themselves responsible by giving bond to the Comptroller-General, from time to time, for suoli limited sums and with such suretics as shall be approved of by the Commissioners, reference being always bad in fixing the amount of seeurity to be so given to the amount deposited therein, and the general transactions of such bank þÿ the trustees may, on the deposit of such secu-

rity, receive deposits on the guarantee of the Government for the repayment thereof. Such are the principal provisions with reference to the Government security to be given to depositors. There are several other clauses in the new Bill, referring to matters of minor importance, with reference to alteration of rules, inspection ofbooks, Ac. As at present, no person will be allowed to invest money in more than one savings bank, or to a greater amount than £30 in any one year, the net interest payable on deposits to be £2 10s. p. a. and no depositor's account is to exceed £200 in the whole.

The 27th clause contains a provision that will be of great convenience to parties whose avocations render it necessary that they should frequently change their place of residence, and is to the effect that deposits may be transferred from one savings bank to another, but no alteration is to be made in the name of the depositor. The 43rd clause provides that in order to give additional facilities to the labouring classes to deposit their savings at interest, and with due security for the repay ment thereof, the eommissioncrs, on application made to them in writing by not less than twenty inhabitants of any place rated to the relief of the poor, and attested by the minister or church warden, ie., may appoint receivers for the pur poses of this Act at such places and under such regulations, and with such security as may appear to them to be proper and necessary, depositors to have the guarantee of the Government fur the repayment of money deposited with such receiver Every institution so managed by a receiver to be considered as a savings bank, with the intent and meaning of the Act, Ac. There is a provision that interests on deposits shall in future be calculated twice a year, instead of once as heretofore ; and lastly, in case of savings banks already established, and which are not afterwards brought within its provisions with reference to the Government guarantee, the trustees are not only to be personally liable for repayment of deposits, but are to place a notice in a conspicuous part of
such bank, that the commissioners <$<!., are not responsible for such deposits CENSORUS.

Amongst the many, who have been severe sufferers in the Danish Capital from the Cholera epidemy, which is raging there, the large number of children, who have been bereft of their parents, are without a doubt not least to be pitied. Christiiuijiilcd, I'roilacii ilen 9de September 1S53. way as through private charity, in order to relieve the immediate wants, still the misery is so great, and the means at hand proportionally so small, that every assistance will be welcome, and will find appropriate application. We beg to direct attention to the appeal made in this number, by Messrs. stenersen, hlngei.beitg ttldemanm of St. Thomas, for charity towards those suffering orphans in Copenhagen, whose parents have fallen victims to that dreadful epidemic þÿ the cholera þÿ which is so direful in its elfects, and commits such fearful ravages wherever it makes its appearance, as to sweep away, within a few hours, hundreds and thousands of people. The number of poor children, thus deprived of their parents or guardians, to whom they looked for support, is immense ; and we read in a late paper, under the head of Copenhagen, that, "the number of children made orphans by the cholera is so great that some of the large rooms at the hotel of the police have been turned into an asylum for them."

Wilmer and Smith's European Times, August 16, 1853. FRANCE. Paris, August 8. þÿ The announcement in the Moniteur of yesterday, that the note of the Four Powers had been accepted by the Czar, made a most favourable impression on the Exchange today. There was a rise of f3 on the lowest prices of Saturday. A curious report is at present current in Paris. It is whispered that preparations arc being privately made for the coronation of the Emperor and Empress at Notre Dame, or the 15th inst. The Emperor, by an imperial decree, elevates M . Drouyn de L'Huys, Minister of Foreign Affairs, to the dignity of Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour, in consideration of his eminent services in the direction of diplomatic affairs. A decree, which bears date the 7th inst., authorises the return of M. Baze to France.

Short Description oflhe Character of the Chinese. Ry most European writers, the Chinese have been represented as the most dishonest people in the world, employing their natural quickness only to improve the arts of cheating the nations with which they deal, especially the Europeans, whom they cheat with great ease, particularly the English, while they observe that none but a Chinese can cheat a Chinese. Duplicity and deceit, it is said, arc notoriously prevalent among them ; the cordiality of friendship is very rare ; true benevolence is far from being the general feeling ; and exterior and mechanical forms arc more attended to than the actual practice of virtue.

extracts from the St. Thomas " Tidende," rela- In our to-day's impression will be found some tive to the Tortola Riots. By correspondence of a more recent date from Tortola, we learn that Martial Law had been proclaimed þÿ that many of the late Rioters were in confinement both in that island and St. Thomas, and that other of the Rioters were during the nights placing in the streets of Road Town property purloined in the late disturbances. We regret to find that our remarks in the last "Gazette," relative to these disturbances, have somewhat ruffled the complacency of those Officials who so discreetly abandoned His Honor the President on the occasion. We are told that they merely repaired to St. Thomas in justice to their families, as they would have been all killed had they remained in Tor- We simply remarked that their valor was neu- tola ! ! ! This we think very like pleading guilty. " tralized by their discretion." We insert in our present issue, the Editorial observations on the recent outbreak in Tortola, which appeared in the " Advertiser" of last rary's statement " that the discontent of the Tuesday, but we do not endorse our Contemporural population of Tortola has been of long continuance." On the contrary we have always understood that the laboring classes of Tortola have been peculiarly contented and well disposed. Political agitation has doubtless, more or less prevailed, in the Colony for many years past ; factious men, without personal respectability or public, position, have, from time to time, sought

to bring themselves into notoriety to attain private ends and to satisfy private jealousies, by haranguing in general terms, and on every possi- j ble occasion, and discanting upon the monstrous evils under which they alleged, the people were suffering from the Government þÿ a Government which in their eyes must necessarily be weak and corrupt because it did not perceive their superlative value and recognise their personal and superponderating influence by taking them within its ranks, and handing over the Reins to their unchecked guidance. Their efforts to beget a spirit of dissatisfaction and resistance to lawful authority have doubtless been well known, and many have misled our Contemporary as to the prevalence of general discontent. These popular haranguers have carried with them, as such men always will carry with them, for the moment,

3 5f» <D Jt l> it X A f 1 8 . the idle, and dissolute, but their insane ravings i did not seem in any way to have affected the generally steady and industrious laborer. We apprehend that, although they may have sown the seeds of discontent, other and more directly efficient agencies will bo found to have been silently at work fanning the flames which have lately broken out with such destructive violence. That any such agency will be traced to the Wesleyan Ministers, we entertain no fear. The antecedents of the Wesleyan Ministry, altogether forbid us to harbor so ungenerous and unjust" a suspicion. We observe that one of the objects of the our contemporary, was " to implore the exertion Meeting in the Wesleyan Chapel, referred to by j ! " of the influence of the Government with the "to lessen the amount of general taxation, which " local Legislature, in order to induce that body J j " was felt to be exceedingly oppressive." Every right-thinking man must, we are convinced, regret that such a meeting, with such an avowed object, should have been allowed to take place in a building set aside for the worship of God, and under the auspices of men set apart for Religious teaching. Taxation has always been a fruitful theme for Demagogues and Political Adventurers to descant upon. It always tickles the popular ear, and will always, especially when presented in a one-sided view, seem, however, fairly and justly distributed, oppressive to the ignorant. Such being the general effect, what must the im- | pression be when the subject is urged upon them

by their Religious teachers ? Our contemporary is anxious that the public should suspend its judgment with regard to the part which the Weslcyan Ministers in Tortola are said to have taken in this lamentable affair. Pre-judgment is always unjust, and we do not, and would not on any account, without the most convincing evidence, allow ourselves for one moment to believe, that men professing to be teachers of Religion, and belonging to a Religious denomination, who have hitherto arrayed themselves on the side of good order, could deliberately set about to instigate open rebellion, and violent resistance to constituted authority. There are, however, certain facts before us, which speak in no mistakcablc language, and we cannot pretend to conceal from ourselves that, under all circumstances, the meeting in the Wesleyan Chapel was unwise, and its promoters justly liable to be regarded as indiscreet. It would take too much space to enter now upon the subject of taxation in the Virgin Islands, but we think it can be shown that, under local circumstances the taxation which falls upon the rural population in our Sister Colony, is by no means heavy or oppressive. We shall have occasion at a future period to consider fully this lamentable outbreak in Tortola, and to lay before our readers, as far as enquiry shall reveal them, the causes, predisposing and exciting, which have led to it, and among these, the question of oppressive or non-oppressive taxation, will probably

be a prominent one. In the meanwhile, we shall give to the public such information as shall reach us through authentic sources, respecting this lamentable affair ; and We can only hope that the sympathies of our readers and fellow Colonists I will be awakened towards the unhappy sufferers, and that relief will be afforded them, through some appropriate channel.

Gigantic Ocean Steamer. þÿ An immense new steamer is being built for the Eastern Steatn Navigation Company, by Messrs. Scott, llusscll, Co., of London, and is to be completed in eighteen months. The dimensions and power of th s ship are intended to be as follow namely, length, 680 feet; breadth, 83 feet; depth, 58 feet, with screw and paddle engines ; aggregate nominal horse-power, 2600. It is to be so constructed as to take its whole amount of coals for the voyage from near the pit's mouth, at a rate not exceeding, for the best quality, 12s. to 14s. per ton. It will carry, besides its own coals, upwards of 5000 tons' measurement of merchandise, and will have 5(H) cabins for passengers of the highest class, with ample space for troops and lower class passengers. Its hull will be of iron, and oi more than usual strength, whilst the mag nitude of its dimensions will afford peculiar facilities for introducing many precautionary measures conducive both to strength and security. The whole of the ship's bottom, and up to six feet above the water line, will be double, and of a ! cellular construction, so that any exter I nal injury will not affect the tightness or the safety of the ship. The upper deck will also be strengthened on the same principle. Separate sets of engines, each j with several cylinders and separate boii- | ers, will be applied to work the screw, I distinct from those working the paddle wheels, so that, in the event of temporary, or even permanent derangement ol

any of the engines, or of either the pad die wheels or screw, the other engines and propellers would still be available, and the only result would be a proportionate diminution of speed and consumption of fuel, thus rendering the chances of any serious delay almost infinitely remote. The result of the directors' calculations is that, after making the most ample allowance for working expenses, depreciation, wear and tear, and insurance, a surjdus remains equal to forty per cent per annum upon the capital invested. This estimate is made on the assumption that the carrying capacity for goods outwards should be oc- . being considerably below cupied at the rate of £4 10s. per ton, present freights, and only one-half of the cabin room occupied, at rates for first class passengers, £65 ; second class, £35 ; and third class, £25, including provisions, giving to each of the respective classes enlarged accommodation, and as suming that only one third of the vessel's capacity would þÿ ward voyage. The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted , Tuesday the \6th August 1853. We copy, from the St. Thomas Times, the following articles, connected with the late Insurrection in Tortola, of which we have already given our readers such accounts as we have been able to gather from authentic sources in this Island. Open fii cite 1 1 ion at Tortola! Road Town set on fire by the Insurrectionists.

We deferred giving an account in our last of the melancholy scenes which were then being enacted in the neighbouring Island of Tortola, in order to avoid the possibility of placing before the public misstatements, which could easily have happened at a time when the minds of the unfortunate victims who were escaping from the hands of the incendiary and the murderer, and arriving here, must naturally have been excited and agitated, and as a consequence matters may have appeared to them in a more exaggerated form than was really the ease. A calmer investigation of the circumstances have not, however, modified the enormity of guilt which has in a few days been perpetrated by the country population of Tortola on the inhabitants of Road Town in that Island. But previously to our giving a description of the fearful acts which were committed in the town, it may be proper for us to allude to the causes, however slender, which actuated the country people to give vent to their uncurbed passions, and by their physical resources to commit deeds which are revolting to hiimnnity, and opposed to the Raws of God and Man. it would appear that sometime in the month of June last, a Bill passed the Legislature of that Island, increasing the tax on cattle twelve cents a head þÿ making the new tax thirty-six cents in place twenty-four cents, which was the former of tax. This additional tax is said to have been laid on in order to raise aii amount of money to ,place in proper condition the Poor House, which was
in a very dilapidated state. From the poriod the law was enacted, the country population continued to view it with a bad grace, and were frequently beard to say that whenever the tnx came

3 ir» Dions: AT 13, to bo paid they would resist it. The 1st of August was the day fixed for the payment of the rural taxes of Tortola, and on that day (Monday) a number of the country people went into town, and proceeded to the Treasury, where they tendered the original tax of one shilling sterling, which was refused by the Treasurer, who at the same time told them that if they had not the whole of the tax, they had until the 10th of the month to pay it, and they could accordingly return home and devise measures for raising the deficit. If we are correctly informed, and wc have endeavored to gain our information from more sources than one, the refnsal to pay the tax did not arise so much from inability as an inclination to resist its payment, and, therefore, the advice given them by the Treasurer was received distastefully, and a great deal of palavre ensued, which not being to the point, nor of any concern to the Treasurer, who had not made the law, he desired the people in a peremptory tone to leave his ofiice, which they refused to do, and two of the men appearing to him to have the most to say, and behaving out of all order, he sought to put them out of his office, when they resisted and struck him several blows ; upon this he called in two constables, who conveyed the two men before a Justice of the Peace, and lie sentenced them to pay a fine of £1 sterling each, or go to gaol for twenty days þÿ and as they refused to pay the fine they were taken to gaol. The whole body then repaired to Government House, and demanded of

the Executive the immediate release of the prisoners ; to this demand they were told to petition, and if their cause was a just one the prisoners should be released. This being an unsatisfactory reply, they stated that they would themselves proceed to the gaol and rescue the prisoners, which threat they were not long in carrying into execution. They, therefore, seized the gaoler, beat him unmercifully, forced open the doors of the prison, and all the prisoners, among whom were some most abandoned characters, left to go at largo. The constabulary force in the mean time repaired to the vicinity of the gaol, and finding the amount of aggression committed, set to with their staffs, when a most severe conflict ensued, in which both parties received severe injuries, the country people appearing to a small extent to have given way, but stated that they would proceed to the country for a reinforcement, and would return and set lire to the town in every quarter. The President apprehending that much danger was at hand, addressed an official note to our Governor, and despatched it with a special messenger who reached here on Tuesday at 8 a. m., wherein he asked for the aid of some of our military, and also addressed a note to J. B. Cameron, Esq., Superintendent of the R. M. S. P. Company here, requesting that a steamer might be placed at the disposal of our Government to convey the soldiers up To this request Mr. Cameron promptly complied, and the steamer Conway was immediately got ready for the pur-

pose, but unfortunately Colonel þÿChads note not stating that the Island was in open insurrection, a delay until the morning after the receipt of the communication took place before sending soldiers, þÿ a delay which every human breast must now deplore, for the insurrectionists did not commence to fire the town until 3 p. m., on Tuesday, and the steamer and soldiery could have reached there by 11 a. m. The Conway having to leave that day with the Windward mails, she could not afterwards be made available, but the Magdalena was placed at the disposal of the Government. It was however thought that owing to her immense size the navigation among the keys would be somewhat difficult, and a sailing vessel was dispatched with the troops. Road Town is now a mass of ruins, and almost every respectable inhabitant of that place of whatever caste is a wanderer in the neighbouring Islands. Saint Thomas, we are truly happy to say, is an asylum

for the larger portion of them, where we hope they may find no reason to regret having taken refuge. It would be next to an impossibility for us to attempt to describe with conciseness the events which took place when the town was being fired, þÿ as the most conflicting and heart-rending statements are connected therewith. It is enough to say that the country people deliberately brought in their bundles of straw, and after the first attempt of resistance offered them by the inhabitants of the town, when one man was killed and several severely wounded, they commenced forcing the Arsenal, or place where the Government arms were kept, which they soon emptied, but as Providence would have it neither powder nor balls could be found there ; it was then evident that the rebels were in full possession, and every member of the town sought to make his or her escape with all possible speed þÿ in doing so, the incidents arc varied, painful and distressing þÿ many people arriving here maimed and cut up, others with the bare suit on their backs, and some without any clothing at all. C0I0112I Chads however manfully and bravely refused to desert his post, and even when matters grew so grave that Mrs. Chads and daughters were in self-preservation compelled to fly, they beseechcd the Colonel to leave with them, but his calm reply was, þÿ I am a Soldier, and I intend to die þÿone. The only other persons in authority who remained in the. town are Justices Haddock and Prinui.e þÿ the former with his family having taken refuge at

Govt. -House. Ry Colonel Chads refusing the mob to leave Govt. -House, that building was saved. Our soldiers, numbering 30 men, under the command of Lieutenant Rosenkrantz, in the Danish packet schooner General row Seholten, reached Tortola at about 7 p. in., on Wednesday, and on shewing a light, the same was answered by another light from Government-House, and Colonel Chads came down to the beach, and told them that the insurrectionists having done their work had retired to the country. The next morning the troops landed with luggage, stores, þÿ V0-, an|l have taken up their position at the Government-House and the School-llousc attached to the Episcopal Church. The instructions to Baron Rosenkrantz were that lie should place himself under the command of the Governor, should that functionary be still on the Island oil the þÿformer arrival s there, but ii not he was to endeavour to assist any of the townspeople desirous of leaving the Colony, and that lastly he should retain possession of the town pacifically if allowed, otherwise he should seek to do so by tbe exercise of the means at his disposal. Among the missiles taken to Tortola by our gallant little troupe, we may mention the tispingot, one of those implements of modern warfare, fearful in its execution, and as a mob corrective deals wholesale destruction. To the moment of our writing þÿ Friday, 2 p m. þÿ we are without further information from the ill-fated Town 1

fikif" To the hour of our going to press (12 þÿo clock) we have no information of an important character to add connected with Tortola There was a false rumour spread yesterday that an English sloop-of-war with troops, had arrived at Road Town, but wc felt when it was told to us that there had not been sufficient time tor a manof-war to get there, lint such will he the ease as soon as the intelligence reaches wherever one of these vessels may be. The Packet General ran Scholten , has just returned, and we learn by her that the insurgents have betaken themselves to the country where they are still continuing their depredations ; hut the town was in possession of the so'.dicry sent from here, and sentries posted at the different points of entrance

After the arrival þÿof the steamer Magdalena, from Southampton, with the European Mails, at 11 a. m., on the 2nd August, the mail-boat Lady MacGregor started about noon, with the usual mails for Tortola, but as sbe neared her destination, she met several boats, tilled with people flying fron the Island, and among them was the Postmaster, who ordered the mail-boat not to go on, as she would be sure to be seized by the rebels, and the master of the boat, a steady, trust-worthy man from Jos Van Dyke, by name Mark Vanterpooi,, thinking best to make sure, returned to St. Thomas, with the other boats, having the þÿPresident s Lady Mrs. Ciiads, with her Daughters, Mrs. Stouo anil family, Mrs. Lewis and family, and many others, on board. The mail was, of course, delivered to the Postmaster, in St. Thomas, and the letters, Ac., distributed by him to those who had arrived. When the refugees reached St. Thomas on the night of the 2nd August, there were so many conflicting accounts of the state of things in Tortola, and so many horrible tales of bloodshed and destruction, that the Superintendent of j to Tortola, and placed at the disposal of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company fitted up the small mail-boat Lady Mac Gregor, of only 5 tons burthen, with a supply of stores, of water, Ac. ; and the Admiralty Agent the steamer Magdalena, Lieutenant Tickell, Royal Navy, thinking it his duty on such an occasion to place himself at the disposal of the President of Tortola, when deserted hy

almost all the Officials, took charge of the boat, þÿ Captain Chapman having promptly supplied her with arms and ammunition, boarding-pikes, Ac., and some brave old þÿman-of-war men, s she set sail, either to assist the gallant Colonel to get away, should he be forced reluctantly to ipnt the place, or afford help to those in distress. In the mean time, while the Lady was being fitted out alongside Captain þÿChapman Ship, s the schooner Sc/ioUen left with our Troops for Tortola, and although she had the start by about one hour, the Lady nevertheless went into Road Harbour with her, and Lieutenant Tickell was the first to land, backed by his little band, armed to the þÿ þÿteeth, and had the satisfaction of informing the President of the assistance sent to his relief by our Government. Lieutenant Tickf.i.i. had some trouble to get the doors of Government-House opened to him, Colonel Chads being unsupported, and obliged to be exceedingly cautious to whom he gave admittance on a dark night. It was not only a great relief to him to see the face of a smart and venturesome British Officer, and to learn he was to have some assistance, however tardy in appearance, but also to get something to eat, his supplies being exhausted. The Admiralty Agent was also of good service in landing all the Troops from the Scholten, by the Lady's assistance, as the schooner in the hurry of leaving this port had taken only very a small dingy boat. Having seen the troops landed, and the Governor well protected, Lieut.
Tickell started for St. Thomas, bringing us the first authentic accounts of the condition of affairs to the Eastward, and he also brought letters for Mrs.

mind at ease as to the fate of her husband. However trifling may have been the services of Lieut. Tickell, we trust they will not be overlooked by the British Government, as it shewed how willing he was to brave danger and discomfort, to perform what he considered his duty. We may mention that during the

3 UN Ui (D 1 A71I8, eight hours he was beating up, the little craft was almost buried the whole time; and to guard against the boat being surprised at night, he slept on deck, with liis little crew beside him. To show how very useful the little mail-boat has been at this time, when a pressing request came down from Colonel Chads on Saturday, at 8 p. m., for a Steamer to convey Despatches to Governor Mackintosh, and the Steamer Magdalena was promptly sent within a few hours direct to Antigua, the little craft again set sail for Tortola, with this information to the President, so that he might know on what to reckon ; also that by daylight on Tuesday Troops could be expected by the Magdalena at Tortola, þÿ the Master of the mail-boat being instructed to place himself under the þÿGovernor or- s ders until the Steamer arrived, when he was to return with intelligence to St. Thomas. On the part of our Government, three schooners have been kept employed between this Island and Tortola since the Rebellion commenced, viz., the General van Scholten, which conveyed the first number of Troops to Road Town ; the packet schooner Vigilant, which brought us a reinforcement of Soldiers from St. Croix, and was immediately dispatched

the Executive there, where she has been lying up to the present time ; and the hired British schooner Aldebaran, which conveyed the last supply of Troops from this place, under the command of Lieutenant v. Bi gel, to join those already at Tortola. The Governor of that Island has now at his disposal from St. Thomas 56 Soldiers 2 Serjeants, and 2 Corporals, with Lieutenants Baron Rosenkrantz. and von Bugel, as well as the packet-schooner Vigilant, lying in Road Harbour. With such an available force, the command of the Island can be retained against the rebels, who could be even punished were it not that Colonel Chads prefers delay till such time as he may obtain information from the Governor-General at Antigua. His Excellency Governor þÿI eddersen has also since dispatched to Tortola from St. Croix, in the schooner General v. Scholten, 50 more Troops, under the command of Captain Meincke. There has in consequence been sent from Saint Thomas and Saint Croix 10(5 Soldiers, 2 Lieutenants, and I Captain in command. A mother having a son whose wicked life had often caused her many bitter tears, called on a pious minister of the gospel, and earnestly beseeched him to request the prayers of bis congregation for the conversion of her abandoned son. The minister expressed the greatest sympathy towards the afflicted parent, and promised that her request should be attended to. Accordingly, on the next þÿLord day, s he published the request of the mother to his congregation, in the following words An afflicted mother desires that the prayers of this congregation should be offered up for the conversion of tier profligate þÿson. While announcing the request of the mother, a few stragglers passing by determined to enter this place of worship to þÿ have a little þÿsport, as one of them said ; among whom was the son of the distressed mother. He heard the announcement, listened to ihe prayers, and felt compunction ; he was induced to sit and listen to the preaching of the Word ; and the ultimate result was that this casual entrance into the house of God and the hearing of the Word, proved to his conversion ; and he lived to become j a useful labourer in the missionary field. That þÿsinner doom s might have been eternally sealed from that day, and the circumstance might have ended very differently, had the pious minister in his blindly directed zeal to promote order, mused the doors of the chareh to be closed during Divine service ; whereas, his casual entrance into church and hearing .

of the Word of life, although at a late period, was the means ot his eternal salvation. As similar occurrences are likely to happen every day, the doors of a church, then, should never be closed against any one during the public preaching oj the gospel, which is intended for all to hear.

(Oil tUMCVIlOA V Mr. Editor ! A few days ago we had a fine exam file of the had application of a good thing. A large number of parents were, on Thursday, summoned to appear liefore the Police-Master, accompanied by their children, for neglect of attendance at the Danish School. As this case lias justly given offence to many parents, a few observations may not be uninteresting if they even only serve to put the matter in a true light. Half measures are worse than no measures at all ; and in the end frustrate themselves. If School-attendance were general on the pa rt of the whole juvenile population, as in Prussia, where the law imposes upon parents the strict obligation of sending their children to School, unless they can prove that they are giving them a proper education at home ; or as in Denmark, where, according to Macculloch þÿ educationis widely diffused, there being very few jiersons, even among the lowest classes, who are unable to read and þÿwrite þÿ if school attendance were so general, then we could see consistency in a strict surveillance on parents, who are inattentive to the demands of the State, in this respect. But to summon parents (and such parents too, who are intelligent men, capable of seeing the necessity of their þÿchildren s attending School, and who voluntarily place them there, and pay for them) to appear before the Police Master, to account for the absence of a child for a day or two from School, while hundreds of children, having the same natural rights, are allowed to run
about the streets, learning nothing but how to become bad citizens and to ruin their souD, is in my opinion the grossest

S <© m <© inconsistency which could ever take place. And then to summon those parents to take their girls and boys, in such a public manner, before a Magistrate is, when we consider the prejudice here existing against the respectability of being called before a Police Court, to degrade those children in their own eyes. In Denmark, where the Ordinance of 1814 upon which this proceeding, 1 suppose, is in a manner founded, School-attendance, as above stated, is general ; consequently this proceeding acts as a wholesome check on ignorant parents, who would, and who only could neglect their þÿchildren good. s But alas ! VVe have borrowed the Shadow and refused the Substance. Why not place Schooling on the same footing as in Denmark, and then let this proceeding follow in due course. It is the duty of the State to educate; if good and not bad citizens are desirable. Be- j port, however, says that Government intends making some alterations in the School System ; but until this is done, 1 am of opinion, that, to compell intelligent parents to bring their children before a Magistrate to account for the absence of those children for a day from one School, and that notoriously none of the best, is a measure which will surely frustrate itself; for, what has been and will be the consequence ? Why parents will, as long as it is optional to them to r do so, place their children at other Schools, where no such regulations will a fleet them. Such regulations may hold good, at present, in regard to those parents,

whose children attend the School gratis; and if we are properly informed, such was the intention of Government, in giving such an order to the Police Master. It is therefore necessary that this subject should be investigated, in order that the like shall not occur again ; otherwise it cannot be difficult to foresee the total abandonment of the School. Yours, B.

Mr. Editor! Do you think there is either sound policy or justice in the way in which Labourers are frequently humbugged and shuffled about from Manager to Administrator þÿ or Owner þÿ and back again from Administrator to Manager; nay, they are often compelled finally to resort to the Police Master, in order to obtain þÿ Passes when they wish tochange their residence in accordance with the Regulations þÿ made and modified in such þÿcase? I equally condemn the shameful and injurious system of intrigue and tampering, which is carried on by planters with each þÿother people s at this season of the year þÿ an unwise practice which all condemn, but one which, nevertheless, mean as it is, there are precious few who dont follow. These people have rights and they ought not to lie cajoled or humbugged out of them by this sort ofartful dodging. Some honest influential persons should raise their voices against both parties, in order to put them down, by which the operation of the laws and regulations would be left fairly to take their course, and in my humble opinion, if properly adhered to, would prove beneficial to all parties. Cure for Sea Sickness. þÿ A writer in the London Times says : þÿ þÿ Having noticed in the public journals a recent instance of death from sea-sickness, under very painful circumstances, I am induced to hope that the mention of a

3 IT '& & 'i SL A T 1 remedy, which was entirely successful in a case which came under my own observation, may be useful to other sufferers from this distressing malady. A lady of my acquaintance on the Cape of Good Hope, was landed at her voyage home from India, in such a deplorable state of debility and exhaustion from sea-sickness, that she was obliged to be carried into the house by men, and would certainly have died if the ship had been a week longer at sea. The danger of renewing t lie voyage under such circumstances was very great, but a simple contrivance enabled her to continue it, and to reach England in perfect health. A swinging cot was constructed, with a top or frame over it, fitted with curtains, so as effectually to screen the deck over-head, and other parts ol the vessel, from the view ot the recumbent invalid. The motion of the ship was thus rendered imperceptible, and the invalid being relieved from the dizzying effect of the vessel appearing no roll one way and the cot the other, to longer felt any nausea or inconvenience. She soon gained sufficient strength to leave her cot for short periods, except in bad weather, and the confinement, such as it was, was a t r l He compared to that which persons who have lost, or dislocated, limbs arc compelled to endure, in pain, for months. At all events, life was saved, and health restored, by this simple means.

One of them, addressed by Count Nesselrode to the Grand Duke, contains the following passage. It is dated St. Petersburgh, Feb. 12, 1830: þÿ The object of our relations with Turkey is that which we have proposed to ourselves by the treaty of Adrianople itself, and by the re-establishment of peace with the Grand Seignior. It only depended on us to march to Constantinople, and to overturn the Turkish empire. No power would have opposed that course; no immediate danger would have menaced ns, if we had given the last blow to the Ottoman monarchy in Europe. But in the opinion þÿot the Emperor, that monarchy, reduced to exist only under the protection of Russia, and to merely execute henceforward her desires, suited better our political and commercial interests than tiny new combination, which would have forced us either to extend too far our domains by conquests, or to substitute for the Ottoman Empire, States which before long would have become our rivals in power, civilization, manufactures, and wealth ; and it is on that principle of his Imperial Majesty that our relations with the Divan are now regulated. Since we have not decided on the ruin of the Turkish government, we endeavour to support it in its present state ; and since that govern-
ment cannot be useful to us but by its deference towards us, we require from it the religious observation of its engagements, and the prompt execution of all our wishes.

The Packet, which arrived here on Saturday last, brought the pleasing inþÿI entligAuction, som afholdes Fre- telligence that the Bill on the Compensadagen den 2den September d. A. om tion Question had passed both Houses, that His Majesty the King had, on the 23d July last, most graeiously given his assent to it. The amount accorded is FIFTY Dollars for every slave emancipated on the 3d July 1848. Compensation will he paid Cash to owners, who had but one slave at the time of emancipation ; but those having more than one will receive payment in yearly instalments at 4 per cent interest, to be reckoned from the 1st July last. It is presumed that it will take about five or six months to complete the preliminary steps indispensable necessary for the issuing of the obligations. This happy result has been brought about through the indefatigable exertions of the present Government, to whom no little credit is due for the zeal they have evinced in promoting the welfare of these colonies, by urging the settlement of this important question. We hope to be able, by the arrival of the next packet, to lay the Bill before our readers.

Louis Napoi. þÿeon s Yacht. þÿ An unplcassnt scene was presented a day or two since at St. Cloud, in consequence of alledged reckless conduct on the part of the captain of the þÿEmperor s new yacht, the Eugenie. This is a pet vessel, built and fitted up at an enormous expense, for the purpose of enabling their Majesties to enjoy the scenery of the Seine. The bed of the river in the neighbourhood of Paris is so narrow and in many places so shallow that it was no easy task to construct a vessel of tolerable size capable of being used for this service. It was soon found that the Eugenic could not he navigated at any great speed near Paris without occasioning a purtnrbation, not only dangerous to smali boats, but injurious to the numerous barges moored in the river, where washing and other occupations are carried on. Hitherto she has gone very slowly on her trial trips through Paris, but the other day her commander, Captain Excelmans, being ordered to bring the yacht to St. Cloud, got up the steam opposite the Louvre, and continued at a rapid rate down the river to the park gates. The inhabitants of the barges were thrown into consternation. Their peaceful stream hud never been before so Jv-turbed Heats broke from their moorings; tubs, bum. . linen were washed overboard and carried down the stream. From the Pont dos Arts to the bridge of St. Cloud both banks of the river resounded with execrations against the Eugenie Several owners of the barges sent in claims for damages, but met with no attention. A few days

later the yacht made another trip near Si. Cloud in a very shallow part of the river, and as it is said, did great damage to property on the banks. The report of what had occurred in Paris had predisposed the St. Cloud people to resent this sort of interference with their vested right, for when the yacht returned to her station, opposite the park, about a thousand people were collected, who assailed Captain Excelmans with loud complaints. A captain of an imperial yacht, you may well conceive, would be little disposed to listen to a rabble on the deck of his own ship, am' ip sight of the þÿEmperor palace. s Captain Exceimans treated the crowd with contumely, and threatened the most turbulent with his voice and gestures. He forced his way through to mount the horse waiting for him on the bank of the river, and his demeanour excited such indignation, that as he rode off the mob pelted him with mud and stones So the matter rests for the present

This latter despatch states that the concessions of the Porte to Russia were of such a nature that the question was considered as all but terminated. Xlic Slave Trade in Cuba. Some highly important information lias been elicited by the Parliamentary Committee now sitting on the slave trade. Mr. J. Eiggins, who had recently visited the Slave Coast, was examined, and he stated that the slave trade was generally increasing in Cuba. The profits of the smaller sugar estates amounted to twenty-five per cent., and of the larger to forty-five per cent. The rum and molasses paid the cost of production, and the sugar was clear prolit. The governor of Matanzas received two doubloons per head, and the deputygovernor one and a-half, (or a guinea and a-half,) for every slave that was introduced there. The Creoles as well as the Spaniards, were engaged in the slave trade. The authorities were also engaged in it. There was no natural increase in the population. The slaves, who cost £75 each, worked from IS to 20 hours a day in the crop time, and they also worked on the Sundays. The crop time extended from January to August. The governor and his deputy were paid by the slave-traders, who carried on their traffic in spite of the British cruisers. The slave trade was connived at by the authorities, and lie believed carried on by them. Sometimes the slaves worked all night. A planter told him that slavery was not a state of existence that secured the greatest amount of human happiness, but lie endeavoured to make his slaves as happy as lie could, so long as it did not interfere with the general system. The present prosperity of Cuba arose from the increase in the cultivation of sugar

and its shipment to Great Britain and elsewhere, the conversion of coffee into sugar estates, and the augmentation of labour through the medium of the slave trade. As much as ,£100,000 was invested on some estates. There was a great deal of American capital in Cuba, and a strong American feeling ; and a planter told him that Cuba would, no doubt, soon become altogether American. Arrangements, when he was there, lie understood, were making for importing some hundreds of thousands of Chinese into the island, which might possibly diminish slavery. The increase of the slave trade in Cuba since 1840 was to be attributed to the change that took place in the policy of this country with reference to the sugar duties ; but so highly did the Cuban planters value their admission to the markets of this country, that he believed, if the abandonment ol the slave trade was to be made the condition of their continued admission, they would at once make the sacrifice. Mr. James Kennedy, for ten years commissioner at Havannah, and a member of the Court of Commission, þÿsaid It was the Spanish who were chiefly engaged in the slave trade but one Forcat, a Frenchman, was one of its most active promoters. The increase that

8 Alt % 3 had taken place in the slave trade was attributable, in a great measure, to the opening of the English markets to slavegrown sugar. It rested with the captains-general to suppress the slave trade, if permitted by the Spanish Government. These captains-general, however, were interested in a contrary direction. The salary of a captain-general, appointed by the Spanish Crown, was £8000 ayear, but the profits they made, in the shape of doubloons, or head-money, amounted to many thousands more ; and one captain-general had retHed, after four years, with a fortune of £100,000. The Spanish Government had continually violated its treaties with this country, and the English Government knew it. As far as the commission of atrocities on the slaves was concerned, there was nothing so atrocious but he was prepared to believe it, and, as a general rule, the slaves were very severely treated. The slave trade might be entirely suppressed if the Spanish Government could be induced to send an honest captain-general out with that intention; and this would do far more towards its abolition than declarations treating slave trade as piracy, or British cruisers on the high seas. þÿ Ibid.

From the St. Thomas Times, Aug. 20, 1853. Lost of I iir American (iris Sarah.

Captain Richard Newman, late in command of the American brig Sarah, arrived here yesterday morning from St. Croix, in the schooner W. E. Packet. He reports that the Sarah sailed from New York on the 31st July, with an assorted cargo, and 300 kegs gunpowder, hound for Curasao. Everything continued well until the 7th August, when it was discovered that the brig had sprung a leak ; Capt. Newman immediately had the pumps to work, but the leak continued gradually increasing until the morning of the 17th, when it gained 3 feet in one hour and a half. Finding this the case, and that the vessel could never make her original port of destination, it was thought advisable for the security of the lives of those on board to bear away for St. Croix þÿ this was accordingly done, and about 2 a. in., on the IStli, she struck oil' the West End of the Island. Whilst endeavouring to get the boats out Ac., the awful cry of Fire was heard, and on reaching the cabin from the deck, it was found to be in a complete blaze, defying entrance. A rush was then made to the boats þÿ all being sensible of the danger at hand, with such a quantity of gunpowder on board þÿ and we are happy to say all hands reached the shore in safety. They had not long been there, however, before the vessel blew up. The captain, mate, and crew numbering 7 men, are at present under the charge of the American Consul here.

From the Saint Christopher Gazette , August 12. By a recent arrival from Tortola, via Saint Thomas, we have received further melancholy accounts of the disturbances which have so unfortunately occurred in that unhappy little community, yet owing to the excitement that naturally prevails on such occasions, we are still unable to give the details with any degree of certainty. They are, however, we can assure our reauers, sufficiently distressing. There appears to have been, for some time past, considerable agitation on the subject of taxation, and we can have no doubt that the riotous proceedings referred to in the extract from the Tide-tide, are chielly owing to, if not altogether suggested by, the indiscreet proceedings of persons in situations which ought to have disposed them carefully to avoid fostering any spirit of dissatisfaction. We are informed that nearly all the houses in the street facing to the Southward have been fired, or otherwise destroyed, and many of the residences in the country have shared the same fate. The Private þÿSecretary Office, s with all the official correspondence, has been burnt ; the Records in the Colonial Secretary and þÿRegistrar Office s have been scattered to the winds, and we arc shocked to add that the Parish Church has not escaped. The rioters made an entry into the building, and destroyed the Parish Registers, Church Hangings, Ac. The majority of the inhabitants of the Town have been compelled to take refuge in St. Thomas lrom the fury of the rural population. The refugees

have bean kindly and generously received by the inhabitants of St. Thomas. The Officer Administering the Government of Tortola (Colonel Chads) has been left in the possession of the reins, which he appears, under the emergency, to have held with unflinching firmness. The Chief Justice, þÿQueen s Counsel, Colonial Secretary, Provost Marshal, reported Privy Councillors to be þÿ no and Legislators, are þÿwhere, þÿ all having disappeared from the scene, evidencing valor neutralized by discretion. This is somewhat in advance, we think, of the lludibrastie distich þÿ þÿ He that fights and ruus away. Will live to fight another þÿday. þÿ many, the Wesleyan Ministers By of Tortola are considered, in no small degree, the authors of the mischief, owing to their having convened, some time ago, a large Public Meeting in their Chapel at Road Town, U>r the purpose of petitioning the Queen to exempt them from local taxation, and to make them a grant for educational purposes. At this meeting it is alleged that some indiscreet language was made use of. We, for our part, acquit the Ministers of any intention to produce mischief, but the conviction is forced upon us, that the course taken by them was altogether blameable. The whole affair will, we presume, receive at an early day a full and searching investigation.

Until then, we shall forbear offering to our readers any further observation respecting its origin. We deeply regret what has occurred, for the rural population of Tortola have long enjoyed the character of being loyal and orderly, a character which they have now forfeited. Severe punishment and heavy retribution will, doubtless fall on the guilty parties. The instigators of this open resistance to lawful authority, must be regarded as the most guilty, however they may have kept from personal par ticipation in any overt act of riot and rebellion.

'J'liE Christian Population oe Turkey. þÿ The population in the dominions of the Sultan is divided into two classes, þÿ the Mahomedans, who are of the number of 17,000,000, and the non-Mahomedans, who are not more than 10,000,000. The latter arc divided into four communities, þÿ the Greeks, the Armenians, the United Armenians, and the Jews. Each community is governed, under the surveillance of the Porte, by a Patriarch, who is at once its civil and religious head, and its official representative with the Government. The Patriarch is named by his co-religionists, and confirmed by the Sultan, who delivers to him a berat, or deed of investure. The Jews of Turkey have as their head a Grand Rabbi, whose prerogatives are the same as those of the Greek and Armenian Patriarchs. The Greek community, composed of all the Ottoman subjects of tlie orthodox (Greek) laith, to the number of about 6,400,000, is divided into two races, þÿ the Greeks, or Romaics, and the Sclavonians, formed of Servians, Bulgarians, and Bosnians. The Greek race is spread over the whole Turkish empire, though in very unequal proportions ; in European Turkey it forms about the eleventh part of the population ; in Asia Minor and Syria, the twenty-fifth ; in three-fourths. chipelago, the islands of the Greek Ar- Amongst the people of the Sclavonian race subject to the Porte are, first, the Bulgarians, whose number is calculated at 3,000,000, who are scattered throughout European Turkey ; then the Servians of Bulgaria,

Bosnia, and the Herzegovine, estimated at 900,000 ; then the Zinzares, a mixed race of Sclaves and Greeks, amounting to about 400,000; and, lastly, the warlike and independent tribes of Montenegro, amounting to 300,000 and making a total of 4,600,000 Sclavonians, to be joined to 2.000.000 Greeks. The Armenians, who reside almost entirely in ancient Armenia and other parts of Asiatic Turkey, amount to 2,400,000. The Jews, who are scattered everywhere, amount to 150.000.

SAGACITY OF HOGS. An English officer, who was in Parts in 1 815, mentioned the case of a clog belonging to a shoe-black, which brought customers to its master. This it did in a very ingenious, and scarcely honest manner. The officer, having occasion to cross one of the bridges over the Seine, had his boots, 'which had been previously to a man who against them. Me, was polished, dirtied by in poodle dog rubbing a consequence, went, stationed on the circumstance having bridge, and had them occurred cleaned. The same more than once, his curiosity was excited, and he watched the dog. He saw him roll himself in the mud of the river, and then watch for a person with well-polished boots, against which he contrived to rub himself. Finding that the shoe-black was the owner of the dog, he taxed him with the artifice ; and, after a little hesitation, he confessed that he had taught the dog the trick, in order to procure customers for himself. The officer, being much struck with the þÿdog s sagacity, purchased him at a high Me price, him brought him to England. kept and tied up in London some time, and then released him. The dog remained with him aday or two, and then made his escape. A fortnight afterward, he was found with his former master, pursuing his old trade, of dirtying þÿgentlemen s boots on the þÿbridge. The dog, however, is not devoid of affection and sympathy for its fellows. Two dogs, near New York, were in the practice of going out together to hunt squirrels on the mountain. One ol them,
in pursuit of some game, got his head

2 W A T 31 3. last between two rocks, from which he could not extricate himself; he remained in this situation eight days, during which time his associate fed him daily. Watch, for this was his name, was observed to whine, and show great uneasiness; he would seize every bone and bit of meat lie eould find, and hasten up the mountain, reserving for himself only the crumbs which were shaken from the table cloth. Me also went often to the master of his friend, and by signs endeavored to induce him to follow him. At length, the master began to notice the conduct of the dog, and one day said to him, þÿ Watch, do you know where poor Alonzo þÿis? 'Flic dog appearing to understand him, sprang up to him with so much force as almost to throw him down, and by other signs induced him to follow him, and conducted him to his imprisoned companion. The poor dog was found to have suffered greatly ; in addition to his being nearly starved, in his efforts to extricate himself he had worn the skin from nis neck and shoulders. Fragments ol the bones which Watch had brought him lay around. Remarkable instances of sagacity are on record respecting this triend of man. .Sometimes he has proved a defense to his keepers in a manner which could scarcely have example. þÿ In been imagined. Take an 1781, a person went to a bouse in Deptford to take lodgings, under pretense that he had just arrived from the West Indies. Having agreed on the terms, he said he should send his trunk that night, and come himself the

next day. About nine þÿo clock in the evening the trunk arrived, and was carried into his bedroom. As the family were retiring to bed, their little house-dog, deserting his usual station in the shop, placed himself close to the chamber-door w here the chest was deposited, and kept up an incessant barking. The moment the chamber-door was opened the dog Hew to the chest, against which it scratched and barked with redoubled fury. They attempted to gyt the dog out of the room, but in vain. Suspicion becoming very strong, they were induced to open the box, when, to their utter astonishment, they found in it their new lodger, who had been thus conveyed into the house with the intention of robbing þÿit.

Crime outwitting itself. þÿ A Protestant clergyman, travelling with his wife in his private carriage through the south of Ireland, a good many years ago, was suddenly stopped by a robber, who demanded his money, his watch, and his þÿwife s jewelry and ornaments, all of which iie proceeded, without ceremony, to lake, menacing the party at the same time with a loaded pistol which he held in bis hand. When he had taken every thing that was valuable, lie permitted the vehicle and its occupants to depart. The carriage had not proceeded far, however, before a second thought struck the robber, and lie gave chase after his victims whom he soon overtook, while the wife was engaged in reproaching her husband for his pusillanimity in not making a determined standagainst the higliwaymftn. þÿ We must change þÿclothes, said the robber. þÿ Strip, and take these þÿ! This was done at once, for the clergyman was a non-resistant, and practiced what he taught. Me was then permitted again to drive on. Mis wife was rallying him upon the sorry figure he presented in the miserable garb of the highway-man, when he suddenly þÿ Rless me exclaimed : ! it is not so bad, after all ! Mere, in the pockets, are all my money,

my watch, and your jewels ! It is all for the þÿbest. 'I'he robber had forgotten, in his anxiety to disguise himself from detection or identification, to empty the pockets he had dishonestly filled, while the very means he had adopted to prevail detection were the cause of his immediate arrest. The minister and his wife stopped at the first inn upon the road, narrated the circumstance that had happened ; a party was sent out in pursuit ; and in less llian an hour the criminal was brought back and secured, having been easily detected by his clerical garb.

Oh! painful condition! Oh ! that things were not so! We want our young men to apply themselves with diligence to the stiid'\ ot things substantial þÿ to give up their aerial aspirations, anil remember that the knowledge gained by reading novels and fairy tales, is merely superficial and intended only ;ts a pleasant pastime þÿ things to he considered hut secondary and which ought only to he read alter one has made himself acquainted with history, with the arts and sciences etc.. and, more particularly with himself. \\ e want to see our young men establish a Society of some description ; where the intellect might lie drawn out, the mind cultivated, and the man fitted to move in any sphere of life. fully at home with their little ones around them þÿ lie aide to relate to them something interesting and instructive. Uz. West End, June 15.

fVilmer and Smith's European Times , June 1 , 1 853. We have advices from Melbourne. The news is highly satisfactory; the produce of the divings continues undiminished. An enormous lump of gold, weighing no less than 1 341 hs. 8 ounces, has been found by four labourers, about a couple of miles from Ballarat. The most remarkable intelligence is the rapid advance in the price of gold, which has brought the exchange on London to par, so that a sufficient quantity of gold coin appears to have arrived to meet the wants of the colony, and the transmission of gold from Europe will probably cease. The pressure of the continuous arrivals of emigrants from all quarters seems very great at Melbourne, and some cases of death from destitution have occurred. The newly-arrived emigrants are directing their attention to other parts of the continent, and Western Australia will receive some of the overflow of beings who cannot find shelter in Melbourne. The þÿafl airs of the East have again become exceedingly clouded, and thecomplications which have arisen, will, no doubt, take further time to disentangle and re-arrange. But as we are strongly of opinion that Russia is not prepared to go to war single-handed in direct hostility to the other powers of Europe, we still cling to the hope, however irritating Prince MenschikofTs proceedings may be, that eventually the dispute will be adjusted Russia may feel annoyed to be compelled to retrace her steps ; but France, in spite of the article which appeared in the Moniteur about the Holy

Places, has, in fact, receded, and Russia must do the same. The alternative risks are too serious to run. It would appear that the concessions granted to the French, as regards Jerusalem, are rescinded ; those for Bethlehem are maintained. The Moniteur has confounded the two, concealing the abolition of the concessions at Jerusalem, under cover of the maintenance of those at Bethlehem. Prince Menschikofl'is seeking, and is said to have obtained, a convention from Turkey, by which the Porte should bind herself not to treat hereafter the question of the Holy Places with any European power, unless with the participation of Russia. So far as the dispute of the Holy Places is concerned the affair is settled, and France and Russia upon that point will each be placed upon the same footing as the other. But as regards the Patriarchate, Prince Menschikoff sent in his ultimate demands, and threatened to leave Constantinople unless they were immediately complied with. He withdrew to Buyuk-dcre ready to leave the Bosphorus the moment his demands were refused. The Sultan remained firm in his resolution, not to part with his authority over his Greek subjects. A complete change in the Turkish ministry was announced, with Rescind Pasha in the foreign department, Mustapha Pasha, Grand Vizier, and Mehemet-Ali Pasha, formerly Grand Vizier, in the war department ; in short a strong Anti-Russian administration. The English and French Ambassadors dispatched messengers to their respective courts for in-

structions, and altogether matters assumed an alarming attitude. Prince Mensþÿchikoff d s emands were, that the Porte should guarantee all the immunities and privileges accorded by previous Sultans, and that Russia should be placed on the most favoured footing as regards the Greek church. That the Patriarchs of Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem, and the archbishops and bishops of the Greek church, should not be deposed for the future, except from a legitimate motive, and that the diplomas

S 'X. « IK <0 a 3t ATJ 3. of investiture granted by the Porte shall receive a full and entire application sin all their clauses. Moreover, that the Ambassador of Russia at Constantinople, and the consuls and agents of Russia elsewhere, shall have the right to protect the Greek church against all kinds of persecution and oppression on the part of the Turkish authorities. That the cupola of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre he rebuilt under the inspection of the Greek Patriarch, and the priority in the tomb of the Church of the Virgin be assured to the Greeks. That the sanctuaries be confirmed perpetually and for ever in the hands of their present possessors; that a church and monastery be constructed at Jerusalem, in which Russian monks shall officiate. It is very evident that the Sultan would, by signing such a treaty, make a complete renunciation of his power over twelve millions of his Greek subjects, and in one word, it would be an abdication of his authority as an independent sovereign. Notwithstanding the accounts put forth of the threatening appearance ofthe military forces at Odessa, the funds continue firm, and no one dreams that Russia will dare to resort to hostilities. However, the affair is serious enough. The French fleet has been summoned to the Dardanelles, and the language ascribed to the Russian Ambassador and to the Emperor of the French is angry enough; but to make the quarrel one simply between the French and the Russians is absurd. Considering the pledge given by the Czar of Russia that he nev-

er contemplated any aggression, but that his demands were restricted purely to the question ofthe Holy Places, it is at present altogether inexplicable why Prince Menschikofl' should have been permitted to assume such a bullying tone, and to embrace in his ultimatum, as the papers choose to call it, demands wholly inconsistent with the independence of the Porte. We have not yet heard ot the departure of the English fleet from Malta, and up to the hour we write, no reliable account has been received of the actual departure of the Prince from Constantinople. In Paris the Eastern question is exciting the deepest interest. The proceedings of the Legislative Assembly attract little interest. It is wholly occupied with matters of domestic interest. The bill relating to the dotation of Marshal þÿNey sfamily has been withdrawn. A bill has passed, sanctioning the formation of a Submarine Electric Telegraph Company to connect France and Algiers, and the concession has been granted lor fifty years to an Englishman. The French Funds have been slightly depressed by the last news from Constantinople. The protracted disputes which have taken place between Austria and Switzerland h ive led at last to the rupture of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and their respective agents have left their posts. It is attempted to be given out that this rupture was occasioned by some personal slight, given to the Austrian Charge þÿd Affaires, but the unsatisfactory state of the Re-

fugee, and other questions, between the two states, is the real cause of the rupture. The Federal Council have published a formal note on the subject. The King of Prussia has left Vienna, and returned to his capital. The King of the Belgians has been received with great eelat, at Vienna. His son, the Duke of Brabant, just eighteen, has, it is said, been actually betrothed to the Archduchess M aria, the youngest daughter of the late Archduke Palatine. There is a rumour that the Emperor of Austria will marry the Belgian Princess, Maria Charlotte, who

is said to be very lovely, but is only just thirteen. However this may he, it is very evident that these alliances between Austria and Belgium must wound the susceptibility of the Emperor of the French, and cannot fail to have an important influence on the future destiny of Europe. The news from Burma!) is of an unsatisfactory nature. There is no prospect of a peace except by pushing forward to Ava. The Burmese Commissioners had refused to sign the treaty. The latest news from China is to the 1 1 th of April, at which date the American, French and English vessels of war on the coast of China, have, at the urgent request ofthe Chinese authorities, consented to guard Nankin, Shanghai, and the mouths of the Great. Canal against the rebels.

ISevivul of the Slave Trade. There is, we fear, no doubt that, so far as the island of Cuba is concerned, the African slave trade is reviving. In spite of the increase of our naval force on its coast, a slaver of unusually large dimensions has been able safely to discharge on its shores not fewer limn 1100 negroes þÿ a cargo worth probably from 400,000 to 500.000 dollars ; and, by the latest accounts from the western coast ol Africa, the slave traders were there, reappearing under circumstances of audacity remarkable even for that desperate confederacy of piratical scoundrels. Vessels, Americ n built, of greater speed and larger size than ever, were being delivered on the coast, where masters and crews are ready to receive and navigate them; extensive arrangements, obviously of some previous standing, had been made for their reception and loading at several of the old slaving ports, where many of the former capitalists or their agents had started up ; and other human cargoes than the one mentioned had, it is known, been þÿ þÿrun. Even in the neighbourhood of Sierra Leone, these unmistakeable symptoms had been observed; and strong apprehensions are entertained that our recent warlike and diplomatic proceedings in the Bight of Benin, and at the ports of Dahomi, and our interference in the internal disputes of Ahbeokutn, so far from really tending to suppress, have reopened a footing for the slave trade in spots where it once flourished. As yet, however, this revival ofthe infamous trade is exclusively

Spanish þÿ a fact established not only by our knowledge ot' what Brazil has done and is still doing in the question, but by the superior capital, organisation, and arrangements which characterise these proceedings on the coast. This circumstance, whilst narrowing the counteracting policy ol' England, increases, in one point of view at least, the responsibility of our Foreign-office. For, as we have repeatedly pointed out, it is neither oil' the shores of Cuba nor on the coast of Western Africa, but in the Court of Madrid, that the Spanish slave trade can be most successfully attacked ; and there, if Lord Clarendon wishes now to nip the evil in its bud, he will insist on its termination, in terms the most peremptory, and language that cannot be neglected. The Spanish slave trade depends altogether on the policy of the Court of Madrid. It did so even when the Cuban planters thought their welfare and prosperity dependent on large annual supplies of Africans piratically imported ; for, during the regency of Espartero, it will be recollected, how completely Gen. Valdez, þÿ when energetically supported and encouraged by an lion. Government in Spain, þÿ checked the trade, and how severely he punished those who dared to violate the laws of

their country. Hut recent events in the island of Cuba itself, the high state of prosperity which it has attained, þÿ and, let us hope, the progress of morality, as well as the advent of well-founded fears and just apprehensions þÿ have of late years produced amongst the proprietary classes of that island great changes of opinion as to the identity ot their permanent interests with the slave trade. It may, perhaps, he deemed a hold assertion, hut is not, we are assured, far from the exact truth þÿ that with the planting interests of the island, the slave trade is not now popular; that its present revival does not emanate from, and is not inspired by, the planters; and that, in their deliberate judgment of their own future welfare, the slave trade ought now to terminate. To what influence and source are we then to trace the renewal of the traffic; and how are we to reconcile this proprietary indisposition to encourage the slave trade with the fact of its revival? The fact, from all that we can learn, appears to he that the Court of Madrid, to which the prolonged misrule of Cuba is so profitable þÿ rather than seriously set about those reformations and improvements in its colonial system, by which only the connexion between Spain and Cuba can he preserved, seeks to strengthen and pro- þÿ mote its interests by giving encouragement and support to that which, in its ignorance and stupidity, it supposes the colonists of tlieir prosperity the slave trade. will regard þÿ as the foundation

And to this general consideration of supposed policy is to he added those special pecuniary considerations which play such important though subordinate parts in directing everything Spanish þÿ he it a projected public company or the administration of a great and noble colony. Thus, though the revival of the slave trade is not an economical or agricultural want of the island of Cuba, and though any great increase of its slave population has become a serious political danger, nevertheless the Court of Madrid in its corruption and selfishness thinks that it can best conciliate the free inhabitants of Cuba to its wretched system of administration, by giving facilities to horde of Spanish (not Cuban) desperadoes import to Africans into the island. The political impetus of the revived slave trade is Spanish; the capital and means by which it is carried on are Spanish; the profits are Spanish þÿ Spanish, we mean, as contradistinguished from Cuban ; and therefore it is we insist that it is in Spain, and at the fountain head of all Spanish miseries, the Court of Madrid, that Lord Clarendon must now assail and attack it. Cuba itself is at present much in the same position Brazil was some three years ago. The current of enlightened public opinion is turning against the slave trade ; and if in Cuba free expression could he given to public opinion, and Cuba had anything like a free press or a rational Government, the result achieved in Brazil would also he quickly witnessed in Cuba. But whilst Spain itself
is in the hands of its present oppressors, the prospects of its principal colony seem hopeless. þÿ Daily News.
