Wili.i amTeli.Out-telled. þÿ A Rhine paper relates the following circumstances as having lately occurred at the town of Speyer. It appears that a weaver, known as the best rifle shot of the district, bethought him of affording a crowning proof of his unerring aim. He, therefore, took his rifle in one hand, and his son, twelve years old, in the other, and then, posting his hoy at the end of an alley in his garden, placed an ordinary sized potatoe on his head, retired fifteen yards, raised his weapon, aimed, fired, and cut the potatoe in two, leav- | ing the child neither scathed nor frightened, so confident was the latter in his father being possessed of a charmed hall. Having talked of this fact to his neighbours, and they doubting the truth of the assertion, the weaver offered to renew the exploit forthwith in their presence, although evening had set in. Thereupon the bystanders, in lien of dissuading the man from the attempt, played I lie part of Gessler, and taunted li i in to the proof. The son was therefore recalled, and placed as before, with a potatoe on his cap, at 15 yards, whilst, it being dark, he steadily held a lantern in his raised hand. The rifle was again loaded, raised, carefully aimed þÿ fired ; and again the unerring bullet cleft the lower part of the potatoe, slightly grazing the cap. The neighbours, who probably never read the heart-rending words which the illustrious Schiller placed in the mouth of Tell when lie was compelled to strike the apple from

his dear þÿchild head, s applauded loudly. Not so the magistrates. They ordered the Speyer Freischuts before them, and after declaring that he must he mad ora heartless brute, ordered him to he fined and imprisoned for five days, with the assurance that if ever lie renewed his perilous essays he should be shut up in a mad house, if he escaped the scaffold for murder.

EXERCISE. There is a little tell-tale muscle in the inner corner of the eye, which, it you your looking-glass touching question it, will deliver a the report into state of the whole muscular system which lies elsewhere hidden in your body. When it is pale, it praises you. Muscular development is, by all means, to he kept down. Some means of holding it in check we have already dwelt upon. Muscular power, like all other power, will increase with exercise. We desire to hold the flesh in strict subjection to the spirit. Roddy exercise, therefore, must he added to the number of those forces which, by strengthening the animal, do damage to the spiritual man. We must take great pains to choke the energy of children. Their active little limbs must he tied down by a wellwoven system of politeness. They run, they jump, turn heels overhead, they climb up trees, if they attempt stillness they are ever on the move, because nature demands that while the body grows, it shall be freely worked in all its parts, in order that it may develop into a framework vigorous and well proportioned. Nature really is more obstinate than usual on this point. So restless a delight in bodily exertion implanted is in the child, that our patience is considerably tried w hen we attempt to keep it still. Children, however, can be tamed and civilized. By sending them unhealthy from the nursery, we can deliver many of them spiritless at school, there to be properly subdued. The most unwholesome plan is to send boys to one

school, girls to another ; both physically and morally, this method gives good hope of sickliness. Nature, w ho never is on our side, will allow children of each sex to be born into one family, to play together, þÿmother knee. s and There ought be educated to at be þÿ one if nature had the slightest sense ot decency þÿ girls only born in one house, boys only in another. However, we can sort the children at an early age, and send them oil to school þÿ girls east, boys west. A girl should be allowed, on no account, to climb a tree, or be unladylike. She shall regard a boy as a strange, curious monster; be forced into flirtation; and prefer the solace of a darling friend to any thing that verges on a scamper. She shall learn English grammar: that is to mean, Lindley þÿMurry notion s of it ; geography, or the names of capital towns, rivers, and mountain ranges; French enough for a lady ; music, ornamental needlework, and the þÿ use of the þÿglobes. By-thc-by, what a marvel it is that every lady has learned in her girlhood the use of the globes, and yet you never see a lady using them. All these subjects she shall study from a female point of view. Her greatest bodily fatigue shall be the learning of a polka, or the Indian sceptre exercise. Now and then, she shall have an iron down her back, and pul her feet in stocks. The young lady shall return from school, able to cover ottomans with worsted birds ; and to stitch a purse for the expected lover about whom she has been thinking for the last live years. She is
quite aware that St. Petersburg is the capital of Ireland, and that a noun is a verb-substantive, which signifies to be, to do, to suffer.

The boy children shall be sent to school, where they may sit during three hours consecutively, and during eight or nine hours in the day, forcing their bodies to he tranquil. They shall entertain their minds by stuttering the eloquence of Cicero, which would he dull work to them in English, and is not enlivened by the l.atin- They shall get

snr% o m a 'i s: a?ib» much into their mouths of what they can not comprehend, and little or nothing into their hearts, out of the wide Stores of information for which children really thirst. They shall be taught little or nothing of the þÿw orld they live in, and shall know its Maker only as an answer to some question in a catechism. They shall talk of girls as beings of another nature; and shall come home from their school-life, pale, subdued, having unwholesome thoughts, awkward in using limbs, which they have not been suffered freely to develop ; and shamefaced in the society from which, during their schoolboy life, they have been banished. þÿ Harriet Martineau.

The Expositor, as a record of the Exhibition, would be incomplete without some notice of the opening ceremonial of Thursday last, which was carried out on a scale of unequalled magnificence and splendor, and was worthy, in every respect, of the august occasion which called it forth. Few' events of modern times have attracted so large a share of public attention as the Exhibition of 1853, which both in conception and execution is unique. All previous demonstrations of a similar character were got up either under the auspices and at the expense of the State, or by associations of influential individuals. On the Continent, where the duties of the Executive are much more extensive than would he sanctioned by the policy of these countries, the management of such exhibitions is entrusted to one of the governmental departments, from the comparatively limited the talists, and operations of private capi- general inadequacy of their efforts for such a purpose. Even in wealthy England, the only demonstration of the kind partaking of a national character, was got up by an association of some of the most influential noblemen and gentlemen of the country, appointed under a Royal Commission, and presided over by the Prince Consort. And although' Exhibitions of Industry have been long familiar to the Irish people on the same premises as that of this year, they, too, have been under the auspices of one of the oldest and most influential

public bodies in Europe, llut, paralysed as Ireland has been by famine, and distracted by party feuds and internal commotion þÿ the object of the sympathy, and it may be added, of the charity of the surrounding nations þÿ it was reserved for an Irishman to achieve a triumph to which either ancient or modern times afford no parallel. That which hitherto had been undertaken by Government or by associated enterprise, was in this case carried out single-handed by one man, not less to his own honor than to that of the country to which he belongs ; and the movement thus originated not only at once acquired the confidence of Irishmen ; hut it also obtained that of her Majesty, of the leading manufacturers of Great Britain, and of the governments and people of several other nations. No wonder, then, that Irishmen should he proud of their Exhibition, and of the patriot by whom it has been founded. To the opening ceremonial people of all ranks and classes looked forward with joyous anticipation þÿ a feeling which was in no small degree increased as the building approached towards completion, and the nature of the arrangements connected with it became known. The beauty of the structure itself, designed as well as founded by an Irishman, and the unequalled treasures which it was expected to display, caused the opening ceremonial to he looked to with a degree of interest without parallel ; and it is not too much to say that the expectations thus entertained were not destined to lie disappointed. While the ceremonial

of Thursday was attended by the representative of the Sovereign, and graced by the presence of a large proportion of the nobility and gentry of the country, it was carried out on a scale which left nothing to he desired Those who enjoyed the rich treat of being present on that occasion, will not soon forget the gorgeous and soul-stirring scene which it displayed. It has been already intimated in these columns that Mr. Dargan undertook the erection of the building himself, in conjunction with the Executive Committee,

3 X. <B lit (0 tt SL AT1IS, I without the intervention of any contractor for it ; and with the well-known punctuality that has characterised the whole of his operations, the opening took place on the day appointed, invitations had previously been sent by the Committee to a large number of official and other distinguished personages, for th<; ceremonial, at which 10,138 ladies j and gentlemen had also secured the privilege of being present, by the purchase of season tickets. From all parts of the United Kingdom distinguished strangers arrived in town, to take part in the proceedings of Thursday, and such was the interest manifested even in the great metropolis, that a special express train left London for Holyhead on the previous day, with visitors to the Exhibition, the journey then performed being the most expeditious on record between the two capitals. During the previous few days unusual hustle and activity were apparent throughout the city, and the 12th being a general holiday, not only at the various public establishments hut also among the merchants and traders generally, and the weather, moreover, having been highly propitious, the streets presented such a scene of animation and gaiety as it is impossible to describe. The doors of the Exhibition were opened to those having the privilege of admission at ten þÿo clock, one of the side entrances being especially reserved for members of the Royal Dublin Society, who were distinguished by wearing their badges. Numbers of anxious visitors at once thronged to catch an early

glimpse of the building, the appearance of which soon became gorgeous in the extreme. The feelings produced on entering the Centre Hall were those of amazement and delight. The noble proportions of the building, the apparently countless succession of arches presented on either side, the vistas between them, which conveyed an idea of almost unlimited extent, the array presented by an orchestra of over l(HM> performers surrounding þÿTelford s great organ, the cheerful and appropriate colouring of the decoration harmonizing so well with all around, the brilliant assemblage of rank and fashion assembled to do honour to the occasion þÿ the tout ensemble thus presented has seldom been equalled much less surpassed. The large number of official personages present was indicated by their peculiar costume, the gay colours of the military uniform contrasting curiously with the dresses ot the judges, and authorities of the university. On entering the door almost the first object that attracted tin

equestrian statue of the Queen, placed in the centre of the hall ; and ranged along either side were massive works of statuary, the colossal statue of Mr. Dargan by Jones occupying a prominent position on the right hand side near the upper end of the hall. The general effect was also much heightened l»v a variety of evergreen flowering shrubs being judiciously interspersed throughout the building. By previous arrangement the members of the Town Council headed by the Lord Mayor went in procession to the Castle to accompany the viceregal party in state to the Exhibition. The knights of St. Patrick were also present in the uniform and wearing the insignia of the order. The display along the route was imposing in the extreme. His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant and the Countess of St. Germans were attended by Major Ponsonby, Private Secretary. &e. <fec. &c. On the entrance of the Lord Lieute- | nant the Orchestra struck up the National Anthem. After a short pause the j Hundredth Psalm followed, and rarely

if ever have the words of the inspired Psalmist resounded with such imposing, such soul-stirring effect. When over 1000 performers took up the words þÿ Willi one consent let all the earth To God their cheerful voices þÿraise, the sensation produced thereby was grand in the extreme, and eminently calculated to rouse devotional feelings even in the minds of the most thoughtless. The well-trained notes of the unprecedentedly large number of performers appeared as if proceeding from some single wondrous voice; and the instrumentation was equally creditable and effective. þÿHandel sCoronation Anthem followed, w ith the introduction of the new words, þÿ Queen of the Isles, Victoria þÿreigneth, which was admirably rendered, the execution fully realising the ideas of the great composer. THE TIMES ON THE DUBLIN EXHIBI- TION. The Dublin Exhibition, though it is not to be seen in its glory till the end of the month, has fairly outstripped its formidable rivals at Sydenham, Paris, and New York. What there is of delay is chiefly on the part of the foreign eontrilmtors. The French, as usual, take a long time to arrange their collections to their own fastidious taste ; the Belgian and Prussian collections are slowly emerging from their cases ; the Mediaeval Court is behind hand, and the machinery is only getting into motion. Already the Exhibition is pronounced to be not only beautiful, extensive, and interesting, but to possess an interest of its own; and they who report this saw enough of the Exhibition in Hyde Park to make them not easy to please. Sitat-home people in this country may wonder to hear that a building of imposing dimensions and of a þÿ tasteful design than the Crystal Pa- rather more þÿlace has been finished so promptly in a land of barren sentiment and dreamy delays. They do not consider that all our own public buildings are mainly the work of Irish hands. In this instance much of the praise is owing to the munificent patriotism of the contractor, William Dargan, one of those great men who will come forward at a national crisis, and not only employ a high order of intellect and vast resources, but risk all they have for the sake of their country. We believe that he will be perfectly content if he is simply repaid the 100, 000/. lie has advanced for the comple-
tion of this work. It would, however, be but poor encouragement if his returns should stop short at that, and we trust that the Dublin Exhibition will prove

8 Vt ® 3t 3S: AT13, as good a pecuniary speculation as that in Hyde Park. There is no reason why it should not. We happen to know that many English people of that class who cannot get on without an annual excursion have so far resolved to make the tour of Ireland, that it is only a question of time, and a very slight thing will be enough to determine them. The Dublin Exhibition is an event the like of which there never was in Dublin before, and which is not likely to recur in the course of the present generation. That city may now be seen in something of that ideal light which her poets and orators have loved to throw around her, as the former resort of learning and the arts, in times when science had to commit her labours to perishable manuscripts, and the arts also wanted those mechanical aids that now perpetuate and multiply their conceptions. Nor can it be forgotten tlmt this is a purely Irish achievement. The Dublin newspapers feel an honourable pride in recording that there has been in this case no parliamentary grant, no aid of any kind from the Royal Commissioners, and, hitherto, nothing from the state, except the viceregal presence at the opening. Such a tact we cannot regard but as an auspicious omen of the moral independence of w hich Ireland at length shows a proper ambition. There is no knowing what people can do till thrown on their own resources. We are glad to observe, too, that while our fellow-subjects across the Channel are enjoying the sense of unassisted exertion, they are not insensible to the noble

part borne by Mr. Dargan throughout this great work, and a complimentary þÿ tributeþÿ is already announced. Hut what is there to be seen at Dublin that was not at Hyde Park? In the first place, the building itself, besides being quite spacious enough to satisfy all but Hrohdignagian expectations, is a more graceful structure than its gigantic original. Then there are the Irish visitors. Does anybody want to see Ireland in a nutshell ? All races, all parties, all creeds and professions, are there seen moving about with as little apparent discord as we used to see between Cardinal Wiseman, Father Gavazzi, the Bishop of London, Mr. Bright, the Duke of Wellington, and others, who met nowhere but in Hyde Park. It will be something to see the lion sit down with the lamb, though where the Irish lamb is to be found, except in the gentler sex we do not happen to know. But there is plenty of Irish beauty, and that beauty knows how to set itself off as well as or even better than in this gaudy metropolis. Besides the peculiarity of the guests, there is also, as we learn, a decided advance in the arrangement, which, in the British half of our own Exhibition, was by no means what it should have been. Everybody remarked on the crowded, stiff, or otherwise unartistic effect of almost every section in the British half, particularly as compared with the French saloons. What Ireland has itself to show that was not exhibited in 1851 remains to be seen, but it can easily be shown to better advantage,

and doubtless also in greater abundance. But there are some features in the Dublin Exhibition entirely new. The most prominent is a collection of pictures contributed from all the modern schools of Europe, and some of them painted expressly for the occasion. We are not aware of any opportunity hitherto afforded for comparing the works of modern European artists, including in that term the present and the last century, except that which we now owe to the interest felt by all the civilized world in Ireland. It may be added, that the other contributions from foreign govern-

ments and nations are quite as interesting as ours, in London, if not quite so extensive In particular may be mentioned a collection of Japanese objects, chiefly from the Hague and Leyden. But nobody desires the same interminable profusion of objects that people attempted þÿ see them in 1851. þÿ Enough, astliey to see þÿ though few did really say, þÿ is as good as a þÿfeast.

The following reflections upon þÿ Unde þÿTom þÿCabin s and the slave question in the United States, are from the pen of a distinguished American, a friend ot the slave and not an anti-Abolitionist : þÿ The effect of the publication of þÿ Uncle þÿTom þÿCabin s in this country is, to me, somewhat questionable. Without a single exception, previous Abolition literature has been decidedly injurious the cause of the slave. Masters hold slaves, as a general rule, either because it is their interest to hold them, or be-

cause they cannot, as honest men, as good Christians, manumit them, to remain in this country, consistently with the þÿslave happiness s here, and his prospects hereafter. Now, abuse neither weakens the influence of interest, nor gives activity to philanthropy ; and abuse or something generally akin to it ; has commonly þÿ certainly up to the date of Mrs. þÿStowe work s þÿ been the weapon of Abolition. þÿ Now, þÿ Uncle þÿTom þÿCabin s is far better in tone than the run of Abolition publications. It is the work of talent, and it is the work of a woman; and although describing mantic way, improbabilities in of has still sufficient a very ro- interest about it as a mere narrative to make it pleasant reading as a work of fiction to slave-holders themselves. 1 doubt, therefore, whether it has been as mischievous as some far inferior productions þÿ mischievous, l mean, to the slaves, whom it is the object of the writer to benefit. I am sure, however, that it has done no good, and am very confident it has done some harm. Its readers, generally have been the congregation of believers in its doctrines. Outside of these I have not heard that it has made a convert or produced an emancipation. It is as powerless to convince an interested man, or to induce a philanthropic one to manumit his slaves in opposition to what he conceives to be their true interests, as the rest of the category to which it belongs. It is like a sermon preached against absentees from church ; those

hearing it þÿdon deserve t it, and those deserving it þÿdon hear t it. þÿ I see that Mrs. Stowe has the promise of much attention in England. I would be proud of this, as she is my countrywoman and a person of talent, were I not afraid that the attention paid to her may be looked upon here as the expression of English feeling which in regard to an institution with generally our people, among whom it exists, brook no foreign interference. I do not believe that the question of slavery, as it exists in the United States, is understood in England þÿ first, because not one person in ten troubles himself about it at all ; and again, because those who do affect to understand it are, after all, very ignorant in regard to it. I do not think Mrs. þÿStowe visit s will tend to enlighten the public mind upon the subject, but it will occupy prominent place in newspaper a columns, which, with greedy avidity, will be reprinted on this side of the Atlantic, and make what may, in fact, be but the act or opinion of a few appear to he the conduct or voice of the whole English people ; and while no one could join more cordially, under ordinary circumstances, than myself in paying to merit its tribute, yet I would hesitate were I to believe that in doing so there would be the slightest chance of prejudicing in the smallest degree the kindly relations that should subsist between countries having so much in common as England þÿ Do not, and the United States. I beg you, understand me as supposing that Mrs. Stowe is to affect

international relations ; but just now, since þÿ the þÿcompromise, since the Preþÿsident i s naugural, I have thought there was more than usual quiet between the different sections of our country in regard to þÿ the slavery þÿquestion, and I look with jealousy upon anything and everything calculated to raise even the tiniest, ripple upon the now glassy surface of a sea lately in such violent þÿcommotion. I, A ItOIC HONOR \ ism:. The man who is able to work and does not, is to be pitied as well as despised. lie knows nothing- of sweet sleep and pleasant dreams. He is a miserable drone, and eats a substance be does not earn. Perhaps he thinks it is not genteel to work. 1 1 is kind ot gentdity is the most worthless and contemptible of all gentility. Had not those before him, near or remote, toiled hard, the degenerate son or daughter would be compelled to earn their bread, instead of being a bogus aristocracy upon property they never earned. One generation labors hard to accumulate property for a generation of simpletons to squander. Persons should he respected tor their virtues and usefulness, hut such drones are not virtuous or useful. There, þÿthat j s ust as good as preaching, and if the priests were what they profess to be, they would have told you of it long ago; but because you drop money into the hat, to be seen of men, they fear offending you, and therefore do not tell you what miserable, good for nothing creatures you are. You think it is honorable to live without work do you ? What would you think of a great able bodied man who would go about the streets wrenching bread and butter from children, robbing old men and women, and cripples on crutches of their garments and wearing them himself, and pilfering or forcing from them their little store of provisions, while carrying them home from the market, and then to hear him boast that this was more honorable than working honestly to earn what he wanted ?

What would you think of such a fellow ? You would call him a mean, contemptible scoundrel, deserving of the workhouse. Well, you are not a whit more honorable, and it is a pity that you have not sense enough to know it. Suppose your fathers are rich enough to support you in idleness, what then? Have they not filched at least a portion of their wealth from worn out men and women? Have they not beaten them down in wages, and charged them too much profit on goods and provisions? Have not children sometimes gone hungry or ragged because of the miserly grinding disposition of your parents in accumulating the wealth that supports you in indolence? Then what better are you, and how much more honorable, than the wretch that would go up and

food, when able to earn it ? You may not get your \ þÿthat as grub through the same process, yet comes from it the same source, you do not earn it, and while you are idling, poor, worn out people are performing the work which you ought to do. Honorable to live in idleness is it ? Well you have a strange idea of honor. It is a pity you do not see yourselves as others see you; for if you did, you would soon be ashamed out of your false notions of honor, if you arc not destitute of shame.

Traffic in Circassian Slaves. þÿ Sarim Pasha, flic Governor of Trebizond, bus, we understand, been deprived of his government through the representations of the Russian Consul in that place, whose complaint concerning some Circassian slaves he refused to investigate. | or þÿroasted. Trebizoud is one of those ports in the Black Sea where Circassian and Georgian slaves are frequently landed. In the Russian territories the seizing and selling of slaves has been long since put a stop to. Parents, however, who wish to send their daughters to Constantinople are allowed to do so under the pretence of sending them to relatives there, and under the guardianship of proper people. In this case each individual is

str, a t a: furnished with a passport. It happens, however, that occasional bands of marauders from Lazistan or the coasts of Circassia, land in Mingredia, and pounce upon the villages, carrying off young girls and children into slavery, in order to convey them to Constantinople, where they find a ready sale at high prices. These expeditions being usually performed in small boats, they are obliged to put in at the ports of the Black Sea for food and water. The Russian Consuls stationed there do their utmost to destroy this illicit traffic. A number of these slaves having arrived a short time ago without passports, the Russian Consul claimed them as Russian subjects, but the Pasha turned a deaf ear to his representations, and allowed the slave-dealers to depart with their cargo, whereupon the Consul lowered his flag, and wrote to Prince Menchikoff, whose influence at the Porte was sufficient to deprive the Pasha of his place. þÿ IVilmer and. Several Ladies also attended the ceremony, and occupied a marquee erected for the occasion. The Meeting having been called to order by Major Wolff, The Reverend J. P. Knox, Minister of the Reformed Dutch Church, commenced the ceremony by delivering an Address, explaining the object of the Institution, and defining the principles of universal benevolence and charity, typified as it stood in works of humanity, evincing the progress of modern civilization, in the steady endeavours of man to alleviate as much as possible the great amount of physical suffering of his fellow-man. In regard to those Institutions, the Reverend speaker pronounced the same ornaments to the age, and that it was a similar object which had drawn together the assemblage then present þÿ and briefly enumerated the advantages in a material as well as moral point of view, accruing to society from similar undertakings; observing at the same time that there could be no difference of opinion as to the great contrast offered by the Institutions of ancient Rome, which represented her boasted grandeur and fame, the instability of which is confirmed by her downfall, as recorded in history þÿ whilst the Institutions of modern times, having for their basis the universal welfare and relief of suffering humanity, can never decay, but will always remain imperishable. The speaker, after appealing to the intelligence of his auditory, expressed his conviction of the value of an Asylum so urgently demanded, and under the most painful

circumstances, owing to the virulence ot a fell disease, which had already caused such fearful ravages among the seamen of all nations ; such a tribute, as now proposed to meet the evil, he thought necessary to a meritorious class of men, for what would Commerce be without the assistance of that class? What would become of Agriculture? What would become of the Mechanical Arts, without the assistance ot seamen? The Commerce of Saint Thomas would languish, would be ruined ; it would at last wither away to nothing ! It will be asked, why such an Institution was not provided for long before this ? Because the sanitary state of these Islands had heretofore been remarkable? Because, under such favorable circumstances, the temporary exigences were provided for in those private establishments which supplied the ordinary necessities of the moment, and where the seamen and strangers received every kind attention; but in the presence of the late afflictions þÿ the scourge þÿ rendered a greater effort indispensable, and in this Asylum will be recorded the result of that effort. In this Asylum the sufferer will find shelter ! In the hour of suffering he will find competent attendance, care and attention, as well as the necessary sustenance; and lastly, it will prove the means whereby the tears of the Widows and Orphans will be dried up, whilst their lips pronounce a blessing on the Projectors of the Institution. Such is the abridged outlines of an excellent Address, which we regret not

being able to publish thoroughly, particularly when delivered with all the fervour which the human heart is wont to bestow on a theme calculated to arouse its nobler sympathies. Mr. Lane, in his Account of the Manners amt Customs of the Modern Egyptians, gives the following story as an illustration of the nature of the local government to which the people of Egypt are subjected : þÿ The nazir, or governor of the soulhernmost district of the Delta, a short time belbre my present visit to the country, in collecting the taxes at a village, demanded of a poor peasant the sum of sixty rials, which was then equivalent to about thirty shillings. The poor man urged that he possessed nothing but a cow, which barely afforded sustenance to himself and bis family. Instead of pursuing the method usually followed when a fellah or peasant declares himself unable to pay the tax demanded of him, which is to give him a severe bastinading, the nazir in this case sent the Skeik el-Beled to bring the poor peasþÿant cow, s and desired some of the fellaheen or peasantry to buy it. They saying that they had not sufficient money, he sent for a butcher, and desired him to kill the cow, which was done ; he then told him to divide it into sixty pieces. The butcher asked for his pay, and was given the head of the cow. Sixty fellaheen were then called together, and each of them was compelled to purchase, for a rial, a piece of the cow. The owner of the cow went, weeping and complaining, to the þÿnazir superior, s the late Mahoir.med Bey, defturdar. þÿ My þÿmaster, said he, þÿ I am oppressed and in misery: I had no property but one cow þÿ a milch cow ; I and my family lived upon her

milk, and she ploughed for me, and thrashed my corn ; and my whole subsistence was derived from her: the nazir lias taken her, and killed her, and cut her up into sixty pieces, and sold the pieces to my neighbours þÿ to each a piece for one rial ; so that he obtained but sixty rials for the whole, while the value of the cow was a hundred and twenty rials, or more. I am oppressed and in misery, and a stranger in the place, fori came from another village ; but the nazir had no pity on me. I and my family are become beggars, and have nothing left. Have mercy upon me, and give me justice : I implore it by the þÿharem. The defturdar, having caused the nazir to be brought before him, asked him : þÿ Where is the cow of this fellah þÿ? þÿ I have sold þÿit, said the nazir. þÿ For how much þÿ? þÿ For sixty þÿrials. Why did you kill it and sell it?' þÿ Fie owed sixty rials for land; so I took his cow, and killed it, and sold it for the þÿamount. þÿ Where is the butcher that killed þÿit? þÿ In þÿMenouf. The butcher was sent for, and brought. The defturdar said to him : Why did 1 you kill this þÿman cow s þÿ?

þÿ The nazir desired þÿme, lie answered, þÿ and I could not oppose him ; if I had attempted to do so, he would have beaten me, and destroyed my house. J killed it, and the nazir gave me the head as my þÿreward. 1 þÿMan, said the defturdar, þÿ do you know the persons who bought the þÿmeat? The liuteher replied that lie did. The defturdar then desired his secretary to write the names of the sixty men, and an order to the sheik of their village, to bring them to Menouf, where this complaint was made. The nazir and butcher were placed in confinement till the next morning, when the sheik of the village came, with the sixty fellaheen. The two prisoners were then brought again before the defturdar, who said to the sheik and the sixty peasants : þÿ Was the value of this þÿman cow s sixty rials V þÿ Oh, our þÿmaster, they answered, þÿ her value was þÿgreater. The defturdar sent for the cadi of Menouf, and said to him : Oh, cadi, here is a man oppressed by this nazir, who has taken his cow, and killed it, and sold its flesh for sixty rials; what is thy judgment þÿ? The cadi replied : þÿ He is a cruel tyrant, who oppresses everyone under his authority. Is not a cow worth a hundred and twenty rials, or more? and he has sold this one for sixty rials: this is tyranny towards the þÿowner. The defturdar then said to some of his soldiers : Take the nazir, and strip him, and hind þÿhim. This done, he said to the butcher: þÿ liuteher, dost thou not fear ('od V Thou hast killed the cow unjust-

þÿly. The butcher again urged that he was obliged to obey the nazir. þÿ Then, said the defturdar, þÿ I order if thee to do a thing, wilt thou do it þÿ? þÿ I will do þÿit, answered the butcher. Kill the þÿnazir! said the defturdar- Immediately several of the soldiers present seized the nazir, and threw him down ; and the butcher cut his throat, in the regular orthodox manner of killing animals for food. 1 Now, cut him þÿup, said the defturdar, þÿ into sixty þÿpieces. This was done : the people concerned in the affair, and many others, looking on, but none daring to speak. The sixty peasants who had bought the meat of tiie cow were then called forward, one after another, and each was made to take a piece ot the flesh of the nazir, and to pay for it two rials; so that a hundred and twenty rials were obtained from them: they were then dismissed; hut the butcher remained. The cadi was asked what should be the reward of the butcher, and answered, that he should be paid as he had been paid by the nazir. The defturdar, therefore, ordered that the head of the nazir should lie given to him ; and the butcher went away with his worse than valueless burden, thanking (lod that he had not been more unfortunate, and scarcely believing himself to have so easily escaped until he arrived at his village. The money paid for the flesh of the nazir was given to the owner of the cow. Most of the governors of provinces and districts, Mr. Lane adds, carry their oppressions, of which the above is an in-
stance, tar beyond the limits to which hey arc authorised to proceed by the ruler ot Lgypt. þÿ Chambers' # Miscellany.

From the Observer, Proposition of the Great Powers. The proposition made by the representatives at Vienna, and which Lord J Russell declared to be acceptable, has not yet been published ; but the substance of it is understood to be as follows. It forms a sort of narrative of the whole affair since the arrival of Prince Menschikoff at Constantinople, and sets forth þÿ first, the transmission to the Sultan of the ultimatum sent by Prince Mensr.hikoff in the name of the Czar; and secondly, the answer made by Reschid Pasha in the name of the Sultan. It then enters at great length into an examination of the difieient questions which have arisen as to the principles on which the differences are to be settled, and the form in which that settlement is to be embodied ; and, having stated the views of the representatives on this thorny subject, it defines clearly what the mediating powers understand, on the one hand, by the protectorate to be given to the Czar, and on the other, by the independence and integrity of the Ottoman Empire. No stipulation is made as to the evacuation of the Danuhian provinces; and indeed any allusion made to the subject in the course of the document is only indirect, it being to all appearance considered improper on the part of diplomatists to express the slightest doubt as to the intentions of a Czar who has pleJged his word of honour that a certain thir.g shall be done.

AUSTRIA- It would appear as if one power, upon whose support the Czar seems to have reckoned, has already deserted his cause. The new attitude assumed by Austria in the negotiations at Vienna has already altered the face of matters. At first Austria held back, and refused to join the other powers in their defence of the Ottoman Empire. The occupation of the principalities by Russia, however, is rather loo strong a measure to be palatable even to the Emperor Francis Joseph. In making common cause with England and France, as she seems lattetlv to have done, Austria gives an amount of strength to the coalition against Russian usurpation that will probably make Nicholas himself hesitate k is stated that iri the conferences which took place at Vienna between the representatives of the four powers, Al. de Boul declare thai he could assure his colleagues that ihe arrangement proposed would he agreed to liv Russia. The probability is that the Austrian Alinister would not have made such a declaration, or even have taken part in the arrangement at all. unless he had in the first place ascertained the sentiments of the Cznr. and found that the proposed convention would satisfy him. It is nevertheless feared that the position taken by Austria, so far from bringing the question to a settlement, will still further involve it Is the vanity ol the Czar, they ask, not at stake? Will he not he irritated still more by finding that Austria, whose empire he kept together, lias joined France and England in the coalition against

him. It will be dangerous to attempt to answer questions which depend on the will of one man, and that a man who is not accustomed to contradiction, or inclined to follow the dictates of reason. All that can be said is that the negotiations are becoming
more and more complicated as they advance, and that the prospects of peace seem every day to recede.

Louis Napoleon and Nicholas. þÿ An article from Al de Laguerronniere, in the Pays , has excited some attention. The object is evidently to show that the policy of the French Government is that of peace þÿ of peace maintained without dishonour; and dint the Emperor, instead of having every moment his ardour restrained by the English Cabinet, has throughout maintained " a calm dignitv." Al. de Laguerronniere maintains that such policy was honourable and wise þÿ and was of a nature to prevent war, or to prepare for it in such a manner as to ensure success From the relations which are known to exist between the court and Al. de Laguerronniere, and the beliel that Louis Napoleon himself inspires similar articles, more importance is naturally attached to them than to others. This article concludes hv declaring that if, as there is every reason " to believe, Russia accepts the propositions made in the name of the four Powers, all is terminated þÿ it is peace. But if, contrary to every reason, and to every probability, Russia refuses, then it is war, but war under the best circumstances ; that is to say, having for its cause a threat and a resistance to all Europe."

THE BEARD AND THE MOUSTACHE. The following observations present the question of the beard and the moustache in a novel point of view. That much more may be said in favour of retaining hair on the face as well as on the head, is beyond a doubt ; but it is not to be doubted either that the custom of shaving is conduciv! to cleanliness among a large class of the population to whom the beard and moustache would be an irresistible temptation to filth ; and that in so far it has its uses. Whether the sanitary effects of the beard and moustache are greater than those of the razor is a point, therefore, in dispute; but whatevei may be the decision, the subjoined remarks will be perused with no little interest : þÿ They protect the opening of the mouth, and filter the air for a man working in smoke or dust of any kind ; they also act as a respirator, and prevent the inhalation into the lungs of air that is too frosty. Air. Chadwick, years ago, was led to the discussion of this subject by observing how, in the case of some blacksmiths who wore beards and inouslachios, the hair about the mouth was discoloured by the iron dust that had been caught on its way into the mouth and lungs. The same observer has also pointed out and applied to his argument the fact that travellers wait, if necessary, until their moustaches have grown before they brave the sandy air of deserts. He conceives, therefore, that the absence of moustache and heard must involve a serious loss to labou ers in dusty trades, such as millers and masons : to men employ-
ed in grinding steel and iron, and to tiavellers on dusty roads. Men who retain the hair about the mouth are also, he says, much

a jn © m <t> a £ ati a. less liable to decay, or acheings of the teeth. To this list we would add, also, that apart from the incessant dust flying in town streets, and insepafable from towh life, there is the smoke to be considered. Both dust and smoke do get into the lungs, and only in a small degree it is possible for them to be decomposed and removed by processes of life. The air passages of a Manchester mam or of a resident in the city of London, if opened after death, are found to be more or less coloured by the dirt that has been breathed. Perhaps it does not matter much ; hut surely we had better not make dustholes or chimney funnels of our lungs. Beyond a certain point this introduction of mechanical impurity into the delicate air passages does cause a morbid irritation, marked disease, and premature death. We had better keep our lungs clean altogether, and for that reason men working in cities would find it always worth while to retain the air filler supplied to them by nature for the purpose þÿ the moustache and beard around the mouth. Surely enough has been here said to make it evident that the Englishman who, at the end of his days, has spent about an entire year of his life in scraping off his heard, has worried himself to no purpose, has submitted to a painful, vexatious, and not merely useless, hut actually unwholesome custom. He has disfigured himself systematically throughout life, accepted his share of unnecessary tic-doleureux, and toothache, coughs, and colds, has swallowed

dust and inhaled smoke and fog out of complaisance to the socical prejudice which happens just now to prevail. We all abominate the razor while we use it, and would gladly lay it down. Now, if we see clearly þÿ and 1 think the fact is very clear þÿ that the use of it is a great blunder, and if we are no longer such a slovenly people as to be afraid that, if we kept our beards, we should not wash, or comb, or trim them in a decent\vay, why can we not put aside our morning plague, and irritate our skin no more as we now do ?

THE VALUE OF ADVERTISING. Advertisers will do well to ponder i ho following sensible remaiks contained in a cheap little book, entitled How la Gel Money ; þÿ .lie feels desirous, poor creature, of ' Whatever your occupation or calling may he, if it needs support from the public, advertise it thoroughly and efficiently in some shape or other that will arrest public attention. 1 freely confess, that what success I have had in my life may fairly he attributed more to the public press than to nearly nil other causes combined. There may possibly he occupations that do not require advertising; hut 1 cannot well conceive what they are. Alcn in business will sometimes tell you that they have tried advertising, and that it did not pay. This is only when advertising is done sparingly and grudgingly. Homoeopathic doses of advertising will not pay, perhaps; it is like half a potion of physic, making the patient sick, but effecting nothing. Administer liberally, and the cure will be permanent. Some say they cannot afford to advertise. In this country, where ever) body reads the newspapers, the man must have a thick skull who does not see that these are the cheapest and best media through which he can speak to the public, where he is to find his customers. Put on the appearance of business, and generally the reality will follow. The farmer plants his seed, and while he is sleeping his corn and potatoes arc

growing. So with advertising. While you are sleeping or eating, or conversing with one set of customers, your advertisement is being read by hundreds and thousands of persons who never saw you nor heard of your business, and never would, had it not been for your advertisement appearing in the newspapers."

Beware. þÿ Punch gives the following as being the experience of a very old man. May it be serviceable : þÿ Beware of listening to a man who says lie ' will not detain you five minutes." Beware of purchasing wine at an auction whicii is described as " late the property ol a nobleman who has gone to live on the Continent." Beware, if you are in a hurry, of getting into an empty omnibus. failures " Beware of a shop that deals in "awful Beware of mentioning the name of Ireland in the presence of an Irishman. Beware of interfering in any quarrel þÿ particularly a matrimonial one. Beware of marrying a woman who has " great expectations." Beware of short cuts when you are travelling; of playing with a man who knows a trick or two at cards ; of buying a horse of a friend; of living near a firework gallery; above all, beware of putting your name to a stamped piece of paper, as much as you would beware of steel-traps and spring-guns, or ot putting your fingers in the fire.

What is a Mile? þÿ Jf a young lady walks she comes home quite fatigued, and " is sure she round the corner of the street in which she lives, has walked more than a mile." It a husband is dragged, a little against his will, to a certain street where there happens to be a bonnet shop, though it is not more than twenty yards, he is morally certain " ho has been taken a mile out of his way, if he has been taken an inch." þÿ It is curious the number of miles a mothor-in-law has walked when having a cab. Besides, miles vary so much. A mistress's mile is generally very different to a servant's þÿ a master's to a clerk's. Auctioneers' miles arc proverbially very short ones when they are " describing a property as being not more than an omnibus upon distance from town," or when they are enlarging the merits of a villa that is " only an easy drive from a railway station." Travellers' miles, on the contrary, are generally very long ones. You will hear a delicate young man, who has just walked his " two thousand miles" just as if he returned from a pedestrian tour, boast of having had trailed a pedometer behind him, and had measured every inch of the road. Panoramas also have a very elastic method of stretching out a mile, which cabdrivers would doubtlessly not object to adopt as their own particular standard of measurement. They talk very glibly of being " three miles long," whereas, if the distance came to be measured, it would probably turn out to be þÿ like cabmen's distances generally þÿ not more

than half. There is another deficiency, too, that frequently occurs with the mileage question. We have known a distance that when a party first went over it was only four or five miles, become suddenly increased to eight or ten at least þÿ the same party þÿ especially if a dinner party had when to go over it again on their way back. This difficulty has been felt so strongly at times that every one of the party has preferred þÿ at that late hour þÿ stopping where he was instead of walking home all that distance. These unnecessary difficulties call for a speedy answer to the puzzling question, "What is a mile r" for hitherto the question has been passed over by our police magistrates, from one parish to another, like a pauper, for the want of a settlement. þÿ Punch

TRANSLATION. Amongst the many, who have been severe sufferers in the Danish Capital from the Cholera epidemy, which is raging there, the large number of children, who have been bereft of their parents, are without a doubt not least to be pitied. Although much has been done in Denmark, as well in a public way as through private charity, in order to relieve the immediate wants, st ill the misery is so great, and the means at hand proportionally so small, that every assistance will be welcome, and will find appropriate application. Trusting to the great benevolence, with which the inhabitants of the Danish West India Islands have ever been ready to succour their unfortunate fellow-creatures, without distinction of nations, the undersigned have

joined, in order to appeal to those of our fellow-citizens, who are able and willing, to contribute their mite to the support of such children in the Capital, as have lost their natural guardians from Cholera. Whatever may be tendered to us we shall be happy to receive, and shall transmit (lie amount collected as soon as possible to the Central Committee in Copenhagen. Should any-body wish their contribution applied to a more general purpose, than the one above stated, it is requested, that such an intention may be stated on sending us their gift. Regarding St. Croix Major Keutsch has kindly promised to receive any contributions, and remit the amount to us. St. Thomas , 6th September 1853. (Signed) A. STENERSEN. ./. C. A. HINGE LB E 11 G. W. From the London " Evening Mail," Aug. 12. I> Eft MARK. The internal condition of Denmark, and the maintenance of constitutional government in that Kingdom, have again excited considerable interest in Europe, partly because the success of the recent arrangements for the preservation of the Danish Monarchy in its integrity depends on the good faith of the King's Government towards the nation at large, and partly from a suspicion that the influence of Russia is almost as actively employed on the passage of the Sound as it is on the passage of the Bosphorus. It appears, however, that very confused and inaccurate notions of what is actually occurring in Denmark have got abroad, arid this confusion has been increased bv the extraordinary misstatements of certain correspoiidentsol foreign journals in Copenhagen. Indeed, so singular is the ignorance of some wi iters on the subject, that the Lex Kegia, by which Denmark was converted into an absolute monarchy in 1601, appears to have been mistaken for the constitution of 1849, and we have been gravely told that the Lex liegia was to be suspended or revoked ; whereas the Lex liegia was a declaration of absolute power nearly two centuries old, which was superseded four vcars ago by the constitution. The Danish monarchy consists of three parts þÿ the kingdom of Denmark, the Duchv of Schleswig, and the Duchy of tlolsicin, each having their own Assemblies. In Denmark Proper this Assembly is the Diet, created by the fundamental law of June 5. 1849; in the duchies

the old Estates of Provincial Councils have been revived. The object of the Danish Government is to promulgate, as soon as it can, a constitution which shall include in one legislative body all these several jiarts of the monarchy, and this constitution will be granted to the nation by the authority of the Crown, alone stands between the provincial animosit ies"of its Danish and German subjects, lint, as the (Town has it not in its power to abrogate the existing constitutions and Estates ol the kingdom and the duchies, the object of the measure brought forward by M. Oersted on the last day of the late session is to reconcile by legal nod Parliamentary means the powers and functions of the existing Diet for Denmark Proper with the future authority of the Parliament of the united monarchy. The draught of a modified fundamental law has, therefore, been laid before the House, and will be taken into consideration on the commencement of the next session, in October. To effect a change in the fundamental law, the bill must be approved by three successive Diets, io which the Government is prepared to submit the measure ; and, if it receives the sanction of the Legislature upon these conditions, nothing certainly can be further from a roup d'etat. Nevertheless, the bill in question, which is a sort of self-denying ordinance to the existing Diet, undoubtedly curtails the powers of this body, especially in respect to those matters which are hereafter to be entertaiued by the Diet of the whole monarchy.

I'hus, the ordinary Diets of Denmark Proper are only to he held in alternate years, and the consideration of questions affecting the Sovereign are reserved to the General Diet. 1 here is, no doubt, a considerable inconvenience in thus attempting to transform an existing popular institution, even with its own consent, into another constitutional body the powers of which are not yet defined, but

s ir <611111 A T IC 3. which is to emanate from the prerogative of the Crown ; and it would be more satisfactory if the terms and provisions of the general constitution were before thecountry. But, on the other hand, the Danish Government has a difficult part to plav. Its policy and its duty are to unite by the strongest ties the several provinces ol the monarchy, and gradually to merge the provincial institutions of each part in the Diet of the united kingdom. The Ministers of the Crown are assailed by passions equally violent and unreasonable on both sides, the Danish party being indignant at the prospect of a closer connexion with their German fellow-subjects, and the inhabitants of the duchies being no less afraid ot Danish ascendancy. But it seems impossible for a bystander to doubt that these prejudices must be subdued if the integrity of Denmark is to be |>reserved; and the late Schlcsvvig- Holstein war ought to have taught all parties a little more forbearance, if the recurrence of that calamity and the destruction of Denmark as an independent State are to be averted. These, however, are questions of internal policy, and we have no doubt they will be settled by the nation they concern: and whether the policy of the Danish Cabinet be right or wrong, we have no reason to suppose that it has been influenced by Russia. On the contrary, the Russian Minister at (Copenhagen has taken every means in his power to express his disapproval of the Ministerial scheme, precisely because it is calculated to

perpetuate and extend to the whole monarchy that constitutional form of government which Russia condemns. In her eyes, the present Diet, with all its defects, which contain the germs of its destruction, is doubtless preferable to a constitutional Government, amended by experience, and embracing the whole interests of the country. Similar misconceptions appear to have arisen with reference to the question of the Danish succession As far as the rest of Europe is concerned, that question was definitely settled by the treaty of last year, and all the necessary renunciations had been obtained for carrying that plan into effect, the claims of the Augustenburg branch being barred by forfeiture. Russia took a prominent pay in those negotiations, and formally sacrificed her own eventual rights, arising out of her connexion with the house of Holstein-Gottorp and the duchies. The succession lias thus devolved upon the Prince of Gluckburg and hichildren, who are also, bv their mother, representatives of the elder line. The heir presumptive has just been authorized to assume the title of " Prince ol Denmark," and, though some delay ocourtcd from the hesitation of the Diet in voting t he law necessary to carry the treaty in effect, the whole measure has now been promulgated, and is in full force. As to the eventual rights of Russia, they arc virtually, if not expressively, extinguished by her own concurrence in this act, for the present heir has two sons alive, and, in the improbable event of the

extinction of his line, the great l'owers of Europe would again be consulted as to the order of succession in the Danish monarchy. The true policy of the Danish Ministry is clear enough; they have to persevere in a constitutional government at home, and to maintain their neutrality abroad. To fail in either of these conditions is to fail in both, for they cannot throw themselves under the influence of Russia without forfeiting the con-

fidence of the nation, and they cannot impair the liberties of the realm without losing theii best claims to the support of the Western Powers. We, therefore, believe that none of the designs imputed to them by their opponents have been seriously entertained, and that the liberty of the Danish People will continue to promote its union and secure its independence.

A Small Business.' þÿ There is no more common practice prevailing among the young men of the day, than that of drawing consolation from the ' seductive weed' and were it not for the fact that, when viewed closely, the matter assumes an aspect of grave importance, which to some extent has been overlooked, we would not deem it advisable to expend a thought on it. How many of our young men expend three, six and twelve cents a day, to indulge his morbid appetite for smoke, without one moment reflecting that they are gradually but surely wasting the basis of an ample fortune. The very lowest sum expended in this manner, say three cents daily would give an aggregate amount with compound interest of about one hundred and fifty dollars in ten years ; or in fifty years, over three thousand dollars. þÿ How many young men in this city expends thrice-told the sum upon which the above calculation is based, and think it a trifle which no ' gentleman' would deem loo large an investment by way of keeping up appearances; and yet, my young ambitious friend, this despised ' trifle' would, if properly used, for, say a period of ten years, foot up $659 ; and in fifty years this trifle has walked with amazing rapidity up to the almost incredible sum of over fourteen thousand dollars ! A nice young man would effect to consider it extremely small business to talk about saving such a very diminutive daily portion as a solitary shilling. Thirty thousand dollars is an aggregate ol the 'currency' that comparatively few of our
young men dear to hope for þÿ a point which the highest flight of their ambition has never reached ; and yet the sum is only the investment of twenty eight cents daily for the period of fifty years.

The A i it Vessel. þÿ What effect the Ericsson vessels, if entirely successful, will have upon the coal regions, has much been discussed. A writer in the Philadelphia Ledger thus answers : þÿ The undoubted effect would be this, viz. : Instead of supplying a hundred steamers, as now, with say 1,000 tons of coals a day, we should be called on to supply 5,000 marine vessels, everything that floats, in fact, with 5,000 tons a day. Besides the land would be covered with caloric engines. The cheapened power would banish land toil, and horse drudgery, and negro slave labour. The grease that keeps one negro would propel a caloric plough of 100 negro-power, and other things in proportion. It is clear that Providence has destined the steam or caloric plough

to be the peaceful emancipator of the slave, whom, lor purposes not otherwise possible of attainment, the same Providence sent hither and bound toj servitude to ensure cotton clothing for mankind. As a general principle our colliers may rely that the greater efficient service can be produced by a ton of coal, the more tons will be required ; or, in other words, the cheaper a thing is made the more will be used, as exemplified in pins, matches, and penny papers. 41

AUSTRIA. Some notice has been attracted to the fact that while the English and French consuls in the Danubian provinces have removed their flags, and have ceased to hold relations with the authorities, in compliance with the instructions of their respective Governments, the Austrian Government has given no such orders, and its functionaries are still at their posts, and exercising their duties as before. There is reason to believe that the attention of this Government has been turned to that point, though we arc not aware that any explanations have been demanded. Austria, to be sure has joined her remonstrances to those of the other Powers on the arrangements between Russia and Turkey, but it is evident that she has, as political persons term it, " reserved her action," and given no explanation. no answer, as to what would be her line of conduct in case of the þÿworst in case Russia refused to withdraw behind the Pruth þÿ in case of war, in fact. Perhaps it is not necessary that Austria should so explain herself, even were the matter formally discussed. She was not to suppose, any more than the other Powers, that the slightest objection could be made to the evacuation of the provinces, seeing that M. Nessclrode declared that they were to be held as a ' material guarantee" only till such time as satisfaction was given; and any supposition to the contrary was entirely superfluous. It is certain that no Power has more reason to dread hostilities, which would before long

grow into a general war, than Austria. The very word " war" is hateful to her ; and it is currently reported in political circles here that the Austrian Minister suffers a sort of moral martyrdom whenever it is mentioned in his presence. This is not to be wondered at. M. de Hubner was, of all the diplomatists at this court, the one who, from the beginning, was most confident of the maintenance of peace, ft is not strange, then, that Austria has maintained her reserve ori the question of war. þÿ The. Observer.
